speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 in connection with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.

Due to the fact that certain provinces are deliberately misappropriating federal funds allocated for medicare through the block funding system for other provincial purposes or projects, and due to the fact that this situation has created a serious erosion of medicare which may lead to the collapse of this important health program for Canadians, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. McCauley):
That the government cease immediately to make federal funds available for health care through the block funding system and restore the good old 50-50 cost-sharing formula until those provinces honour their obligations.

Mr. Speaker, recently-on Wednesday, October 24-in the Senate, in answer to a question put to him on Canadian import quotas of chicken, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said:
I will endeavour to inquire from my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, the exact reason why the chicken import quota was set where it was.
He also said:
-the actual negotiations of an import quota such as this falls under the responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture.
He also said:
In terms of representations by the producers' group, I would expect, again, that those representations were probably made to the Minister of Agriculture. They were not made to me.
Will the Minister of Agriculture now tell the House if he was present when the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency presented a brief on the chicken import problem to this government in August and whether he did, in fact, negotiate the entirely unacceptable import quota with the United States, as published in the news release on the 22nd of last month?

Mr. Speaker, in response to the former minister's question-and I want to recognize the fact that the former minister is taking on the physical shape of his predecessor, the agricultural spokesman for the former official opposition-I must say that I, personally, was not present when the presentation of the brief was made.
However, in the intervening time 1 have had many opportunities to discuss this matter with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and, indeed, with other ministers in the cabinet and also with people in the industry. I do not have to go into the problem associated with the negotiations on the level of imports of the commodity between the two countries. No one knows that situation and those discussions any better than the former minister.
I want to say, as well, in response to the former minister's question, that certainly I am not happy, by any stretch of the imagination, with the level of U.S. chicken imports. However, someone has indicated we have sold the Canadian chicken industry to U.S. interests. The House and the country should know that we were sold down the river in 1974, 1975, 1976, 1977 and until we took office on June 4, 1979. Since then we
Oral Questions moved as rapidly as possible, and it is a week ago on Sunday evening that we were able to impose border controls on chicken imports, thus reducing them from about 60 million to 65 million pounds down to 45 million pounds.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the minister has not answered the question. He did not say whether he had the authority, which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in the other place said he had, to do the negotiations. He has not acknowledged this fact. He sounds as though he does have some responsibility in negotiating chicken imports.
In view of the fact that chicken producers have responded to the government's request to increase production in 1978 and 1979, with the result that there are 124 per cent more chickens in storage now than a year ago, will the Minister of Agriculture confirm that, in fact, one Stuart Campbell negotiated the quota as an official of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and that this same gentleman was accompanied in this task by some functionaries of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and that no minister took any direct part in these negotiations?

1 am surprised to hear that type of information coming from the former minister, because he knows very well that when you negotiate import levels on any commodity you have, as part of the negotiating team, representation from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Department of Agriculture, and also the Department of External Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, again the minister has passed the buck. He is not saying why he did not involve himself in these negotiations which are of the utmost importance to Canadian poultry producers, to Canadian agriculture, in Canadian trade deficits and, indeed, to all Canadians who are subjected to increasing energy costs and interest costs. Can he state why he did not deem it necessary personally to protect the jobs and production capacity of a most important section of our economy at the ministerial level?

Talking about passing the buck, may I remind the former minister that he and the former government passed the buck for at least 12 months, and perhaps 24 months, until the time we took office on May 22, and when 1 assumed responsibility as Minister of Agriculture on June 4 we acted properly. We accepted our responsibilities and we placed into effect import controls on chicken.
Hear, hear!

Ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

November 1, 1979
Oral Questions

subtopic: REASON QUESTION OF CHICKEN IMPORT QUOTAS WITH U S. NOT SUBMITTED TO GATT
REASON QUESTION OF CHICKEN IMPORT QUOTAS WITH U S. NOT SUBMITTED TO GATT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. The predecessor of the Minister of Agriculture concluded an egg import quota with the United States that is far more favourable to Canada than the United States chicken import quota accepted by this government.
Can the Minister of Agriculture tell the House why he did not refuse the Americans, in view of the fact the Americans knew a national agency would be established sooner or later on the basis of the principle that a national chicken marketing agency was accepted in May of 1974? Can he state why he did not submit the United States demand for this destructively large quota to GATT arbitration on the basis of pre-1974-figures? His predecessor submitted the Canadian case for the egg importation quota to GATT against the wish of his officials and the Americans, and won.

subtopic: REASON QUESTION OF CHICKEN IMPORT QUOTAS WITH U S. NOT SUBMITTED TO GATT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member might not be aware of the fact that it is clearly stated that the national agency must be in place and operating for one to keep in line with international trading laws and to negotiate a level of imports of chicken or any other commodity.
We did not have National Farm Products Marketing Council certification for the national board until about August 27, 1979. Therefore, it would have been simply impossible to negotiate a level prior to that time. In fact, we were communicating with our United States counterparts in Washington prior to the national board receiving its certification from the National Farm Products Marketing Council.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ONE PER CENT LIMITATION ON CHICKEN IMPORT QUOTAS
REQUEST FOR ONE PER CENT LIMITATION ON CHICKEN IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a question was put in the standing committee of the House about the unacceptable import quota and the minister answered, and 1 paraphrase, that he had acted according to the best advice received and that he did not want to risk American reprisals. Does the minister have so little faith in the stance adopted by the Canadian government as to refuse to ask a limit of 1 per cent on import quotas? Is he also supposing that GATT would not decide equitably on a justified Canadian request?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ONE PER CENT LIMITATION ON CHICKEN IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a great deal of faith in the advice I have received from the officials within my department. I have a great deal of faith in the officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and also the Department of External Affairs- because they were all involved in that particular question. The best advice I received from these officials was the fact that we
should negotiate in good faith. We have done that. That is the only information I can supply to the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Mr. William Daniel, president of Shell Canada, is reported in today's press to want a guarantee of up to 20 per cent profit if it is to proceed with the very important Alsands project in the north. He also said that an agreement is very close to being reached with the federal government.
Considering that this company made $150 million in profits last year without paying one cent in federal taxes, and has just reported a third quarter profit increase of 110 per cent, will the minister assure the House that the federal government will not give one penny in further handouts to this company for this project?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that we are not in the process of giving handouts at all. We are in the process of discussing with a consortium of companies interested in developing this very important heavy oil sands development the appropriate arrangements by which this particular project would be viable.
The fact of the matter is that it involves many, many aspects. But it is a very important development for the purposes of ensuring supplies for Canadians in the years ahead, one which I am sure will receive the support of the New Democratic Party, rather than the negative approach it has taken to all development in Canada up to this point.

Mr. Speaker, the minister talks patent nonsense, and I think he knows that. Considering that Petro-Canada has experience in tar sands work through Syncrude and can get the required equipment, the capital for financing and can do the Alsands project work without any need for profits in that part of its activity, because it is a Crown corporation, will the minister explain to the House why the government does not use Petro-Canada for this fundamentally important development project-and I agree with the minister in that regard-at virtually no cost to the Canadian taxpayer?
Oh, oh!
Instead, he is embarking upon paying corporations billions of dollars in handouts to do it. Can he answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it difficult to answer questions by the Leader of the New Democratic Party because

November 1, 1979

his premises are usually false and wrong. What 1 am saying is that there is a very substantial cost involved in this particular project. It does involve a consortium. Discussions have taken place with respect to this matter, by myself with representatives of Alsands. One of the points I have been making to them is that we are very much interested in increasing Canadian participation in this project.
That is the objective to which this government is dedicated. The purpose of this government is to increase Canadian participation, and I can assure the hon. member that is a purpose I will undertake with a great amount of effort and endeavour.

Mr. Speaker, I want to be factual in my questions and I hope the minister will be frank in his answers. No one is denying that there are important developmental costs; that is agreed. Since the minister has at his disposal a Crown corporation with experience in tar sands work and is not under an obligation to make profits, like a private company would be if it were to do the development work there, why does he not use the Crown corporations, and get a little tough in terms of tax policies with the multinationals in the way the United States government recognized was necessary in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all I can say to that particular proposition is that there is now at hand a consortium, and in respect of the holdings and the development of particular oil sands in Alberta we are anxious to go ahead at the earliest possible time.
I simply say that in terms of profits, and so on, the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party is always complaining, suggesting that Petro-Canada should in fact somehow keep profitable areas of development, but is not interested in Petro-Canada making a profit. I do not understand the logic of his argument. The fact of the matter is that we are going to develop this project to the benefit of all Canadians by ensuring our supply, by ensuring a fair and reasonable transaction, and by ensuring that there is Canadian participation in this. I assure the hon. member that this will, in fact, take place.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PROVINCES CONSULTED RESPECTING CHICKEN IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of State for International Trade if he can tell the House why this government is imposing on chicken producers an import quota of 48.5 million pounds for next year, which will be raised to 62.5 million pounds for 1982, an increase of 14 million pounds? subtopic: FIRST INTERIM REPORT ON COMPREHENSIVE AUDIT OF GENERAL AND FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATIVE SYSTEMS

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FIRST INTERIM REPORT ON COMPREHENSIVE AUDIT OF GENERAL AND FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATIVE SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Order. I should like to take a moment before proceeding to Routine Proceedings to inform the House on a matter which I consider to be of great importance related directly to the administration of the House and indirectly to our spending estimates for future years.

November 1, 1979
Administration of the House
The administrative duties of the Speaker represent an immense but little known aspect of his responsibilities, and when I assumed this office five years ago I am quite certain that my reaction was very much the same as most of my predecessors: first, some surprise at the enormity of the administrative task; second, serious concern about my own qualifications in the administration field, a concern which the House shares, I am sure, since to my knowledge no Speaker has ever been chosen on the basis of administrative expertise- neither has the Clerk of the House nor the Sergeant-at-Arms, with whom the Speaker shares these duties-and yet, we have neither comptroller nor professional administrator within the ranks of the House of Commons staff.
The subject is further complicated by the dramatic and rapid expansion of the operation of Parliament in recent years. For example, 15 years ago the budget was a fraction of its present figure, and telephone privileges, travel privileges, staff, office accommodation, constituency offices and television within the chamber as we now know them virtually all came into existence in that short period without concurrent upgrading in our administrative practices or administrative skills. Members will not be surprised then to learn that the former Clerk, Mr. Alistair Fraser, Sergeant-at-Arms Col. Currie, Director of Administration and Personnel Georges St-Jacques and I were all in agreement that a thorough review of our administration would be of great value.
Against this background, last winter, in keeping with the spirit of spending restraints announced by the government in the summer of 1978, I asked the management and members' services committee to review our estimates in a somewhat different manner than had been previously attempted. We first identified a number of areas in which costs of operations might be reduced, some, but not all, of which would result in reduction of service to members and in turn, through members, to the public.
1 invited the committee to examine our officials on these so that when I presented the estimates for approval in mid-winter, the committee could pass final judgment. Quite appropriately, after taking advantage of the opportunity to examine the officials of the House, the committee concluded that before attempting spending cuts in any major way it, too, would prefer some sort of independent study of our administration. Although we were agreed, neither the committee nor I could begin to formulate terms of reference for such a study, yet we were equally agreed that some start should be made, if possible during the dissolution period.
We agreed to seek advice from the Auditor General and after several consultations with him during which-and I want to underline this to members-his advice was in every sense positive, constructive in its tone and, in my opinion, absolutely invaluable in the steps we are proposing to take. After these consultations, upon which I commend the Auditor General most sincerely, I wrote to invite him formally to begin the process of a comprehensive audit with the hope of identifying administrative weaknesses and recommending solutions, either with or without the help of outside consultants.
[Mr. Speaker.)
The Auditor General very kindly responded to that invitation on my part by putting together a team which started work on the project at once, continued through the dissolution period and, in fact, is still continuing its work. The Auditor General has provided me, under date of October 31, an interim report on that, and 1 propose to table my invitation to the Auditor General of April 4, 1979 and, in turn, the interim report of the Auditor General, his findings on our administrative difficulties and some proposed suggestions for rectifying them, that being his letter of October 31.
In that letter the Auditor General proposes as a long-term solution the addition to our senior staff of a professional administrator and a comptroller. My response has been positive, but I naturally insist on behalf of the House that before any final decision of this sort be taken, ample opportunity be given to members for study and for comment, not only on the exact responsibilities of such an official or officials, but also on their relationship with Parliament, with the Speaker, with the Clerk and with the Sergeant-at-Arms. At the same time, we all feel that an early start on the work of such administrator is highly desirable, since we soon will be asked to approve cost estimates for spending programs of Parliament in the future.
I am therefore pleased to advise the House that the Auditor General and 1 have been able to come to an interim solution which I hope will be seen by all members to accomplish all objectives to the maximum possible extent. The Auditor General has kindly offered, under secondment, the services of the very distinguished Deputy Auditor General, Rheal Chatelain, to serve us as acting or interim administrator, an offer which, after informing House leaders, 1 have readily accepted and for which 1 accept full responsibility.
Mr. Chatelain's duties will be to oversee implementation of administrative programs, and he brings to the position a background which ideally suits him to the task. This interim period will enable us to benefit from his expertise immediately, but also will give to members of the House of Commons the opportunity for study and for comment upon the possible ultimate responsibilities and relationship of this administrator with the other officers I have mentioned.
I want to thank, first of all, the Auditor General for his assistance. He has at all times acted not only as the professional accountant that he is and, of course, the Auditor General of Canada in that immense responsibility to the Canadian people, but he has acted at all times as a servant of Parliament, and his attention to our problems-but, more important than that, his devotion to this institution-has been readily apparent to me throughout all our consultations. I therefore extend on behalf of the House special thanks to him for his counsel and guidance through this period of time.
In addition, I thank the previous officials of the House- Mr. Alistair Fraser, the previous Clerk of the House; Colonel David Currie, our previous Sergeant-at-Arms; Mr. Georges St-Jacques, Director of Administration and Personnel throughout all these discussions; our new Clerk, Dr. Beverley Koester; and General Gus Cloutier, our new Sergeant-at-
November 1, 1979

Arms. All have been most helpful throughout all our consultations.
Lastly, 1 thank the members of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services of the last Parliament, and particularly its very distinguished chairman, the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates), for their wise assistance and counsel during all the preparatory steps which led to the initiation of this interim solution and interim experience for us, with the assistance of the Auditor General and now with Mr. Chatelain.
1 am sure I speak on behalf of all hon. members in expressing hope. 1 want to say, having initiated this collaboration with that committee, that I will be appearing before that committee at a meeting scheduled very soon in order to continue discussions and consultations on this in case there are any questions members want to put. I hope they will avail themselves of that opportunity at that time.
I want finally simply to say that I hope that in taking these steps I am expressing the hope of all members of the House of Commons that in this way we will maximize the opportunity for members to participate in this decision and to discuss it before a final implementation is made; and that in the interim we will be working together with Mr. Chatelain to ensure not only the smooth functioning of Parliament in all its responsibilities to the Canadian public, but, above all, that we will be doing that in a manner which remains exemplary to the Canadian public in our accountability for the expenditure of public funds.

subsubtopic: CANADA STUDENT LOANS ACT-AMOUNT PAID TO THE GOVERNMENT OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
1.	In the past five years, was approximately $59 million paid to the government of Quebec under the Canada Student Loans Act and, if so, what was the basis upon which the payments were calculated?
2.	What is the approximate loss ratio on loans to students in provinces other than Quebec?
3.	What is the average turnover time for student loans?
4.	What is the estimated percentage of the total amount of loans outstanding, at any one time, that would be necessary as an annual contribution in order to maintain the present level of lending?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Diane Stratas (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: CANADA STUDENT LOANS ACT-AMOUNT PAID TO THE GOVERNMENT OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
1.	Yes. Section 12(2) of the Canada Student Loans Act sets out the method of calculating the amount of alternative payment. In short, the amount paid is the proportion of the costs to the federal government in respect of loans made by participating provinces that the 18-24 year age group in Quebec bears to the same age group in participating provinces.
2.	From August, 1964, to December 31, 1978, the loss ratio on loans to students in provinces other than Quebec was 0.14 per cent.
3.	The maximum repayment period permitted under the act is ten years from the date a borrower ceased to be a full-time student. The Canada Student Loans Act and regulations provide, however, that the minister may extend this period in exceptional circumstances. Within the ten-year maximum the repayment period in each case is determined by the lender (chartered banks and other lending institutions) in consultation with the borrower and is dependent upon the size of the debt and the borrower's ability to make payments. There is provision for a revision of agreed terms where a borrower is unable to continue to meet the payments because of unemployment, ill-health or other temporary situation. The bulk of student loans are repaid within six years.
4.	The Canada Student Loans Act is not a self-financing program so that repayments are not sufficent to cover issue of new loans in any year. The act sets out a specific total loan provision for a base year and provides for escalation of that basic loan provision in subsequent years in accordance with the change in post-secondary full-time enrolment in Canada. Total loans advanced in any year may not exceed the loan provision for that year. The act provides that the federal government shall pay interest charges on all loans advanced so long as the borrower is enrolled in full-time post-secondary education at an eligible institution and for six months after ceasing such studies. The act also provides that the federal government shall guarantee lenders against losses due to default in repaying loans. The cost to the federal government in each year is, therefore, the interest charges on outstanding balances of loans for students still enrolled (and six months thereafter) and the paying of claims for loss submitted under the guarantee in that year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please, When the committee rose last evening, clause 38 of the bill was under consideration and the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood had the floor.
On clause 38-Small business deduction

Mr. Chairman, last night we were dealing with the very important clause involving the rights of certain individuals to incorporate themselves and take advantage of the preferential rate which currently exists in the Income Tax Act of
Income Tax Act
Canada. I should like to take this opportunity to go through the history of this particular problem in an attempt to get some answers from the parliamentary secretary respecting the changes introduced by the Minister of Finance in the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice.
In 1972 when the so-called tax reforms which provide the basis for our Income Tax Act were introduced, the Income Tax Act provided for a special reduction in the standard corporate rate for small businesses which qualified as being active businesses. That section of the act has been amended to the extent that now a corporation with an income of less than $750,000 a year receives a special corporate rate, a special small business rate for Canadian small business of 25 per cent, as opposed to the standard corporate rate which is now 46 per cent. It introduced an important incentive for which there is justification.
We pointed out that the majority of Canadians are employed in small businesses and the important role played by small businesses in the Canadian economy. We all recognize those factors. Like so many features of the Income Tax Act, individuals took advantage of this clause. They saw the Income Tax Act as an opportunity to avoid taxation where it should be paid, not as setting out principles to be followed.
What happened to the act? The definition of "active business" income was so extended by judicial interpretation that it provided an opportunity for many individuals to take advantage of the act, individuals for whom the advantages originally were not intended. Unfortunately the courts were complicit in this activity.
It is important to realize the advantages of an active business income and being allowed to incorporate. Those advantages are substantial, as are the tax savings engendered by incorporation. One problem was that a large number of doctors, lawyers, dentists, chartered accountants in provinces where they were allowed, athletes, entertainers and many other professionals took advantage of the small business provision in order to lower their effective rate of taxation.
Also it is important to realize that the fairness of the tax system was no longer evident. As I pointed out yesterday, employees bear the substantial burden of the Income Tax Act.
I am referring to those employees who work hard every day, whose income tax is taken away at source, who do not understand the Income Tax Act and who are not in a position to take advantage of the deductions, special incentives and grants given through the tax system to self-employed individuals and corporations, be they public or private.
There were two good features in the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice. One was the closing of the loophole and the other was the belated decision to come to grips with the problem of term preferred shares and the manner in which banks were taking advantage of them to reduce their effective level of taxation to around 10 per cent. As members of Parliament we all know that the decision of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice to define an active business and a business which would qualify for the lower tax rate, the special small business rate, in such a manner as to exclude profession-
Income Tax Act

November 1, 1979
als such as athletes, entertainers and others in the management service field, aroused a considerable response from a very well organized lobby. I was on the receiving end of this lobby, as 1 am sure were many other members.
The effect of the change would have been to destroy a haven. It would have required doctors, lawyers, dentists, accountants and others to start paying taxes as if they were not incorporated. It would have changed their effective rate of taxation. It would have increased their effective rate of taxation and made it more comparable to that paid by other non-incorporated individuals, be they self-employed or employees.
I am disturbed, as are many others, that the only change, apart from airport tax, the Minister of Finance has made to the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice is to create a third category of corporation and a third standard rate for a special group of individuals. There were no changes to simplify the act, to make it more comprehensible, to make it more fair and to eliminate some unfair advantage given to one group over another. The service group defined in the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice is now being given a special deduction from the standard corporate rate of 12% per cent; it brings them to an effective taxation rate of 33% per cent. But it still allows that group to take advantage of the dividend tax credit, tax deferrals, build-up of credits in corporations and all advantages given to private Canadian corporations in our Income Tax Act.
I have a very simple question for the parliamentary secretary. Despite the mumbo jumbo in the statements of the minister that this tax has a neutral effect, is it not the case that it still will be to the tax advantage of professionals to incorporate rather than not? If that is the case, what is the social justification for allowing lawyers in Alberta to incorporate themselves while other lawyers cannot? What is the social justification for allowing some self-employed individuals to incorporate themselves and take advantage of this special rate while employees cannot take advantage of these incentives?
In his statements on this act before the House, the Minister of Finance said that there were parts of it he was more enthusiastic about than others. But I assume from his press release that since this is the only change, this is the amendment of which he is particularly enthusiastic and proud.
We are entitled to an explanation when we look at the comparative advantages being given to one group of individuals over another. We are being provided with an additional complexity rather than a simplification of the Income Tax Act.
It gives an advantage to people who have the talent and ability to know how to incorporate themselves, those who have particular skills and to whom such a tax bracket is advantageous.
In view of the fact that it was indicated in the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice that it was never intended that this group would be able or be allowed to take advantage of this measure, and that it was only through a series of interpretations that gave rise to this loophole taht was finally closed by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, I think we are
(Mr. Rae.]
entitled to a clear explanation from the parliamentary secretary as to why this has been done.
There is one other point I should like to make. We have this phantom opposition over here in the Liberal party. If members of that party really believed in the importance of fairness in the tax system, we would have some Liberals here who would be prepared to defend that budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice. That is not the case. Those hon. members have backed off. There is not one measure in this budget they are prepared to defend, talk about or intervene on behalf of, or even make an effort to understand. I can understand the braying and the catcalling by members on the other side because they want to get this bill through quickly. It is not in their interest to try to understand it. They know which group they want to give an advantage to and which group they do not want to have the advantage. I can understand that attitude on the part of Conservatives. However, this pathetic performance on the part of members of the Liberal party has to be seen to be believed. They are not here and they do not care about a measure that has been changed. The hon. member for Saint-Maurice does not even have the presence to speak to a matter which he originally thought about and wanted to present to the House of Commons. He has not made a statement about its being changed. The hon. member for Windsor West did not mention the change once in his speech concerning the Income Tax Act. In fact, he did not mention one provision of this measure.
I think it is important that Canadians know that a particular lobby can be mounted after a budget in the dying days of a Parliament and so influence the Conservative party that it brings about a change in the Income Tax Act to provide a special advantage through a loophole to that group of professionals and others who can take advantage of the laws of incorporation to reduce their effective rates of taxation.
We note how concerned the Liberals are about that. They have not said a word or uttered a peep or mutter about this aspect of the budget or about any other aspect of it. I think it is becoming increasingly clear to Canadians who the real opposition to the new or old Conservative party really is. That opposition certainly is not coming from the Liberal party. I think it is clear it is coming from the New Democratic Party. I would like to hear some explanation from the parliamentary secretary in response to our representations.

I can assure the hon. member that the spokesman on this bill for my party will return to the House very shortly. He is presently giving a television interview, so I do not think that the hon. member should make such comments.
1, too, would like to question the Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance on this very strange business of creating a special kind of taxpayer, as the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood describes it. People who have the tax withdrawn at the source, and this includes most people, are the people who pay most of the taxes and who pay them at the very least arguable rates. These people do not get a chance to argue or make claims on expenses. They simply get the pay cheque with the money removed. I am sure that most of these people will resent bitterly a society which gives the guy down the street a special rate because he happens to be a professional or in a tax category which gives him a special tax rate.
It is not the small businessman who is being considered in this clause. The whole purpose of the changes was to give a tax benefit to what all of us understand to be small business, because it is small businesses in Canada which employ the largest number of Canadians. The small business is involved in everything from manufacturing to the retail level. They have felt for a long time that they have been discriminated against in the tax system. They work longer hours, but they always seem to get the short end of the stick when it comes to the tax system.

November 1, 1979
Income Tax Act
There is the belief that it would be advantageous to the country because small businesses employ more people if they expand. I realize that the parliamentary secretary has a background in big business with regard to the oil field. He may not be aware of the plight of the small businessman, and 1 am not saying that in an unpleasant way. Small businesses traditionally have not wanted to get very large. They have enjoyed the kind of activity in which they were involved, but they have always felt that they were being beaten in the tax system.
Over the years the small business tax advantage has been put into the system to create employment. We have found that it is being used by people who are really not small businessmen according to the original concept, but who were, for example, in legal partnerships. As I understand it, and I am not a lawyer, in some provinces the law society will not allow a lawyer to set himself up as an incorporated business. Perhaps the best example is the hockey player who sets himself up as a company and pays his salary into a limited company, thereby paying a smaller amount of income tax. Many people think that this is unfair.
1 recognize that there is a certain amount of tightening up taking place in this clause. I recognize that the hockey player will no longer be able simply to pay his salary into a limited company, but would probably have to claim that he was doing personal appearances or something else besides just putting his salary into a limited company. That represents some small improvement.
I believe that the original changes proposed by the minister of finance in the last government show the direction in which this government should be heading. It should be trying to make income tax payable on a more equal basis and getting away from these special categories. I recognize, and I suppose it will continue to be the situation, that one could have a large income from stocks and other investments which one could pay into a limited company. As 1 understand the proposal, such a company would now be required to employ at least five people. That proposition was proposed by the last minister of finance, and I believe that it is being maintained.
What I do not understand is the way in which the government has caved in to this lobby of people with basically high incomes, in so far as 1 can make out, and who do not want to pay the normal income tax. There are enough schemes already available to these people to divert their incomes. There are special tax rates in this country for the film industry, and for the oil industry particularly with regard to exploration, to mention but two examples. There are a vast number of ways in which a person can get away from paying tax so long as they are interested in creating employment and investing in some sector of the Canadian economy.
1 wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether this proposal has been thought through. As I understand it, if a person puts his money into a company and pays tax at the rate of 33 per cent, that company can accumulate over a period of years a reserve of up to $750,000. I should like to know if it is true that the person who then retires and collects the income from $750,-

000, which could be up to $35,000 a year, would not have to pay any tax on it. As I understand the proposal of the government, it would lead to a situation where people in this country who earn $35,000 per year through income or from dividends or from their company could end up not paying any income tax. That is a pretty serious state of affairs, and I am fairly certain that it is so. I strongly urge the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary to consider that they are creating a potentially new brand of taxpayer.
Every taxpayer in Canada who is paying income tax at the source, and that is most of us-members of the House of Commons have it taken out of their pay cheques like everyone else-anybody who receives a pay cheque, should strongly resent a system which creates a special kind of taxpayer, that is, one who is not paying his taxes.
I then ask why I should pay taxes at pretty high rates. 1 am a single person with no dependants who pays a high rate of tax. Why should 1 pay up to 50 per cent in Ontario? I have the Clarkson Gordon 1979 tax rates here. I have never resented paying income tax, but on behalf of anyone paying their taxes in the normal fashion 1 register the strongest protest against a system which will create a group which does not have to pay or who can avoid paying. 1 would suspect that in the marginal rates there will be many who will not be paying 17 per cent of taxes. That is a disgraceful situation.
It is no wonder that at a time when Canada is getting poorer every year and when the brunt of this economic hardship is being carried by people who do not have any special tax advantages, the individual who has a lot of tax advantages absorbs a lot of the decline in real income in this country, and 1 suspect this is so in most of the world. He absorbs it because he charges it up to the government. The country pays; the other taxpayers pay for him. There could be some person earning $50,000 or $100,000 per year, yet he is being subsidized by someone earning $15,000 per year. That is what is being proposed here. It leads to a situation which I checked today with the Department of Finance. I am not an accountant and my taxes are simple enough that I have never had to understand these various dividends and credits and things that exist for those who can take advantage of the tax system. I never understand them because I can never take advantage of them.
I should like the parliamentary secretary to tell us whether it is true or not true that this can result in an individual having an income up to a maximum of $35,000 per year, so long as it comes in the form of dividends from a dummy company that the person has set up for $200, and not pay any income tax on that amount.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for a few moments on this clause. As a member of a profession for whom this legislation was primarily designed, I might say that putting the rate back at 3316 makes it about as neutral as it can be.
November 1, 1979

The hon. member who just sat down pointed out that dummy corporations have people who get money out of them through wages that they basically do not earn. Many small businesses have people on their payroll who, strictly speaking, might not be considered productive. This seems to be one of the disadvantages of tax systems.
One of the problems that has come from this is the high margin of income tax rates that we have. If the marginal income tax rates were not so high, this sort of thing would not occur so much. Without some provision like this, say with limited liability, it would be almost impossible for physicians, for example, to hold property in groups and to have facilities. Most provinces do not allow physicians to incorporate their incomes; certainly Manitoba does not. I realize that Alberta does allow professional people to incorporate their incomes, but it has probably changed the rules to some extent.
I have considered this over many years and have discussed it with my accountant at various times but I could never see where it paid to incorporate a medical practice, except for the limited liability aspect. For instance, if four doctors decided to build a facility for $150,000 or $200,000, they would pretty well need to have a company to do so. It would have to be organized on a partnership basis. In any case, the tax changes of 1972 made partnerships almost impossible to carry on on an income tax basis if there was any complexity. Most accountant firms will advise against partnerships of almost any kind. As I say, the 331/3 is as neutral as can be.
The hon. member who just spoke implied that all physicians and all professionals were pretty well assured of an income. Mr. Chairman, they are no more assured of an income than the corner grocer. Physicians and lawyers who work on a salary for a firm must pay income tax just as we do. It is not necessarily true that many will come in the door demanding to be paid high salaries or be provided with a high income. I might say that in a practical sort of a way the physician in Manitoba makes about $10 or $14 per hour before taxes. Ele makes up for some of this by working 50 to 60 hours a week. Whether that is too much, I do not know.
I would to like to point out there are many professions, such as pharmacy, which are not included in this. In practice, however, pharmacists can incorporate their companies. They have to be able to incorporate because of the large stock they carry and so on. Usually about half of their income can be classified in the same way as incomes of lawyers and physicians.
If everything went very well and circumstances were exceptionally favourable, it might be that a person could use the 331/3 per cent and make considerable money. However, from my discussions with many physicians, I find they have tended to lose on this. By and large their companies have not been around for a long time. They have been holding companies or real estate companies.
It would be almost impossible to get facilities without having some kind of company. Presumably we would not have
Income Tax Act
clinics and this sort of thing where there is a physical facility. Physicians have told me that having a company has not particularly resulted in their making money. In many cases, their income has been less than had they paid the marginal rate.
The limited liability feature, the possibility of bankruptcy, suits for injuries and so on make it necessary for professionals to be able to set up companies of some kind. This may not be the best way to do that. I have gone through the white paper on taxation of 1970 and subsequent legislation. As a professional, I do not particularly ask for favours. However, something has to be set up in order that facilities can be built and manned.
Another problem that remains unsolved is those who have spent long years preparing themselves and do not earn money until they are in their thirties. They presumably then earn a high income and pay a great deal in tax. Obviously that is a difficult problem. While this change may not necessarily be the best, it seems the most neutral we can arrive at for the moment.
I would ask the parliamentary secretary whether this effective 331/3 per cent rate commenced in November of last year, or will it become effective when this bill is passed, or, in fact, is it effective at the present time?

Mr. Chairman, the question of reducing taxes or customs tariffs is indeed very interesting and leads to heated debates, in this House and elsewhere, the points of view often differing widely. I listened to the former speakers very closely and, though I represent a riding in which the majority of voters are workers, I also represent a number of professionals whose point of view I must also submit to the House and to the parliamentary secretary who is piloting Bill C-17.
I think all we want, we being members of the House, is justice for all taxpayers, a justice which enables governments to collect the money they need to run the country. For this purpose, it is necessary to collect more from those who earn more. But, Mr. Speaker, these laws should not cause injustice under the pretence that everybody should pay income tax. I would like to pass on to the parliamentary secretary some sensible remarks which were written to me by one of my constituents of Jonquiere, Dr. Blais, who states in all deference that in its present form the bill is unfair. In his budget, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, the former minister of finance, had proposed some amendments which were suspended and which this government now wants to implement. Therefore, I would like him to know the remarks of Dr. Blais, and I quote;
The government and the new Minister of Finance, Mr. John Crosbie, plan to amend the tax laws concerning administrative corporations for professionals and companies affiliated to corporations without legal constitution. These would no longer be entitled to reduced tax rates.
We strongly believe that these amendments are arbitrary and that they discriminate against us professionals for the following reasons:

November 1, 1979
Income Tax Act
1. The government proposes that doctors, dentists, lawyers and accountants not be entitled to the reduced tax rates granted to corporations even if they are incorporated. (At the present time, Alberta is the only province to authorize the professions to incorporate, but it is expected that the other provinces will provide this authorization shortly.)
This clearly discriminatory legislation isolates the members of the four major professions and submits them to an arbritary taxation system. If it is passed, optometrists will pay lower taxes than ophthalmologists, chiropractors will pay less than general practitioners, administrative advisers less than accountants and denture manufacturers less than dentists, to mention but a few examples.
2. Moreover, the government wants to deprive most administrative companies which offer their services to a non-incorporated company of the right to benefit from the reduced tax rates generally granted to small Canadian businesses. In fact, if the administrative company offers its services only to a group of professionals and their associates, it will not have this right.
This other measure will be more unfavourable to the dentist who has a company to take care of the administrative side of his practice than any other businessman who might do the same. The government forgets that the dentist incurs higher costs for his equipment and his office and after has higher financial risks than small businesses in general.
It can perhaps be said that not all incorporated companies should benefit from reduced tax rates. However, we see no reason to deprive of this right the companies which take care of the administration of professional practices, whether for dentists or any other major profession. We also think that those provisions should be looked at again and that the government should postpone their passage until such time as more reasonable solutions have been found.
First of all, I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary why, in paragraph (f), on page 49, the non-qualifying business is being limited to the professional practice of an accountant, dentist, lawyer, medical doctor, veterinarian or chiropractor, and why all professions are not included generally; why is this statute limited in that way? Second, why does he, on behalf of the government, plan to deprive administrative business, that supplies services to companies that are not duly incorporated, of the right to use the reduced rates usually allowed small Canadian businesses? Finally, 1 ask the parliamentary secretary whether he has really looked into all other possible solutions to that important matter, whether the decision of the government is final and whether, if this bill having become law proves to be unfair, he will be willing to suggest to his government that it amend it in order to avoid the injustices pointed out by that voter from my riding?

My intervention will be brief, Mr. Chairman.
I need some information from the parliamentary secretary in order to fully comprehend the impact of this proposal upon our existing income tax laws. 1 am bothered by what I consider to be a flagrant violation of the principle of tax neutrality. 1 might say I was not very happy with Bill C-37 either, so it is not a question of my supporting one and not supporting another. But are we doing the right thing by providing this new special rate of 33lA per cent for a particular category while excluding others from similar benefits? Are we paying sufficient attention to the position, for example, of wage earners?
In his own press release the Minister of Finance states on page two, in paragraph three, that such corporations which

retain earnings in the business will still enjoy tax deferrals since the rate of 331A per cent is lower than the personal income tax rate on taxable incomes in excess of $15,000 gross. So here we are proposing in the case of, say, two professionals that in one instance a taxpayer will be paying tax on income in excess of $15,000 at a rate which the incorporated professional will not pay until his income reaches $150,000. This does not strike me as being a just situation from the point of view of wage earners. This leads to an underlying problem which I raised the other day with regard to the very tax rates themselves. Something has to be done.
I say, further: why single out these professionals? There is in this House a fairly representative group of the professionals we are talking about. We even have a well known chiropractor on this side of the House. I happen to be a lawyer. What distinguishes these gentlemen, say, from an engineer or an architect in terms of the proposal which is being advanced? In other words, why does one kind of professional income become entitled to an advantage which other kinds of professional incomes do not enjoy?
Turning to another consideration, we have to ask ourselves: what is the tax cost likely to be? Has the Department of Finance calculated what the tax deferment would be if every professional in this country, every professional who is listed, were to incorporate? The list covers accountants, dentists, lawyers, medical doctors, veterinarians and chiropractors. Let us assume that if this law is adopted a great deal of pressure will be placed upon professional organizations in each province to permit the incorporation of professionals for tax purposes, because given current rates of inflation tax deferrals become very significant. Tax deferred for 10 or 20 years is, in fact, tax not paid.
It can be said that in the long run the tax would be the same. The hon. gentleman said it was neutral. It is neutral if the dividends are declared or the salaries are paid out, but I submit this would not happen because these vehicles would become holding companies for all these professionals. Would the tax cost run into the millions? Or billions? I imagine it would be very substantial.
Getting back to the principle of tax neutrality, is it right for us to create a situation where provincial law will determine what the federal tax rate would be? In my own province, Quebec, lawyers cannot incorporate, accountants cannot incorporate, engineers have techniques for incorporation effectively, but professional societies, as hon. members know, have long resisted incorporation in certain jurisdictions because of the so-called client-professional relationship. It bothers me that we could have a professional in one part of the country with an income identical to that of a similar professional in another province, yet one would enjoy a substantial tax advantage over the other because one professional might be able to incorporate while the other could not. That is one departure from tax neutrality. The second departure is that we have singled out specific professions for preferential treatment.
Now let us consider the position of the ordinary wage earner. Why should he not obtain some sort of deferral? Why
November 1, 1979

should he be subjected to full tax on his income in excess of $15,000 while other salary earners, other professionals, have this opportunity for substantial benefit through deferral? All this leads me to suggest that the approach being taken to corporations and the use of incorporations in this area is unduly complicating our tax structure and must inevitably lead to situations which are completely unjustified in terms of tax neutrality, a principle with which I am sure we all agree. We may disagree about rates. The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood, for example, might like to see us all employed by the state or he might like to see rates of 75 per cent or 80 per cent. But 1 know we would agree on one thing at least: everyone in the same circumstances should be paying the same amount of tax. The hon. gentleman is asking us to approve a provision which would make this objective more and more difficult to achieve.

Mr. Chairman, there are a couple of questions 1 should like to raise on this clause. I must say I found the comments of the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount interesting and informative. The background he enjoys brings to this House an expertise to which 1 think we should pay attention.
There are two matters about which 1 would like to speak, although it was my original intention to address myself to just one. In light of the fact that the particular profession to which I enjoy the privilege of association has been mentioned on numerous occasions today, there are a couple of matters within the ambit of that profession which 1 would like to set straight on the record. I am speaking of my own profession as a chiropractor.
I would like to say that I have been in practice for 25 years.
I have served for two years as the president of the British Columbia Chiropractic Association. I spent nine years on its board, served as a vice president of the Canadian Chiropractic Association and some years on its board, and for some years as a director of the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College.
Having said that and having indicated my dedication to my profession and to the welfare of Canadians, I would like to point out that in the interval, as a member of Parliament- because 1 was elected as a member, 1 resigned as an officer of the profession to avoid any semblance of conflict of interest-I have no hesitation as a parliamentarian, with a background in that profession, in speaking out at this moment. Because with reference to this bill and to this clause, 1 have received submissions from lawyers, accountants and dentists in my community and, of course, my constituency. I have received submissions from medical doctors, but I have not received any from any chiropractors. Nor, to my knowledge, has there been any organized effort by my profession on a national or provincial level to seek any special or favoured treatment in terms of this bill.
Unlike any of the other recognized healing professions in Canada, the chiropractic profession receives not one dime of federal or provincial tax revenue for any programs. It receives absolutely nothing. It has made requests but been rejected.
Income Tax Act
The only area in which there is income accruing from the federal and provincial treasuries is medicare, through insurance programs and through compensation boards. That applies from the province of Prince Edward Island-the maritime provinces with the exception of Newfoundland-right through to British Columbia. We have applied to the Medical Research Foundation for grants for research, and those grants have not been forthcoming.
So what has the profession done? It has raised its own money. It has done so itself to conduct its own research. There is a facility in Toronto which is second to none in the world in terms of educational standards and the quality and calibre of its lecturers. Doctors from Sunnybrook Hospital, lecturers from the University of Toronto and others teach at the CMCC. The profession pays the bills. We pay them to teach our students. Our graduates support that college, and it was only a few months ago that we finally burned the mortgage on that building. That plant is worth some $2 million, and it was paid for by less than 2,000 chiropractors across this nation. So I speak with a degree of pride when I say that we have not come to the public trough except for research, and in that regard we have been denied.
I also want to reiterate the fact that we have not asked for any special privileges whatsoever in terms of this bill.
Having set the record straight on that, there is another matter which 1 find unfortunate. In dealing with the income of corporations for the year under "non-qualifying business , I see listed "prospecting". I see nothing which provides an opportunity for any kind of windfall for the prospector, who is an independent soul. In my mind there are two people with whom I am acquainted who are in the category of a free spirit. One is the trapper and the other is the prospector. I cannot imagine any other occupation in which the individual concerned is more isolated from human contact than those two. Hardships are tougher for them than for anyone else in North America.
The trapper, particularly in the winter months, and the prospector, especially during the summer months, put up with a great deal. Sometimes they are flown in by a company. Sometimes prospectors are paid by a company to prospect in a particular area, but sometimes they have to pay the shot themselves. They are flown to a location and they put on their backpacks. They have their supplies with them and they are in the wilderness for weeks. Wilderness can be pretty tough whether it is in northern Quebec, northern Ontario or anywhere in the mountains of British Columbia. The record shows that most often it is just once in a lifetime that a prospector strikes it rich and makes a windfall discovery. When prospectors do that, those gnarled, hardworking creatures of nature get shafted by the federal government in terms of taxation.
I know a prospector in Nelson right now who is in his seventies. He gets his old age pension; big deal! He is blind in one eye. He walks with a very pronounced limp because one of his legs was shattered as a result of a dynamite explosion in some rock work. He has emphysema because he breathed mine dust in the old days when he was a miner working in areas of

November 1, 1979
Income Tax Act
high silica concentration. This prospector has problems breathing. He has a bad heart and, of course, with his heart and his lungs being in rough shape, this does not make life any easier for him. However, he found his once-in-a-lifetime windfall, and what did the government do?
Not this one.

I refer to hon. members opposite when they formed the government. I am not kidding hon. members; this is all on file in my office, if they want to see the records. They taxed this prospector's windfall away. There was not a tear from the then minister. He could not have cared less about the condition this poor old gentleman was in.
Hon. members opposite do not know anything about human factors. They never take them into consideration. They say, "It is here in the book, and that is what we will go by". That is the problem with any big government. There is a total absence of any recognition of any human factor beyond what is in the book. I pray to God that this government will show some sensitivity in these areas.
I can think of all kinds of other examples, and I am sure other hon. members can too. I think of a person with multiple sclerosis three weeks away from qualifying under the Canada Pension Plan. She is to the point where her MS no longer allows her to do any work. It was to hon. members opposite who formed the government that I appealed on four separate occasions. I must ask, will this government recognize the fact that it should be doing something for this woman-after all, she did make her contributions-even though she was only three weeks' short of qualifying, instead of having her on the bread line? I do not think that is really what governments intend in the legislation they draft.
Let me conclude by saying that I feel it is incumbent upon the parliamentary secretary to consider that a prospector who provides opportunities for the mining community to operate in the fashion it operates should be allowed a once-in-a-lifetime windfall profit, because, if not, the next thing we know there will not be any more of these free spirits. If you look at the record and at the statistics, Mr. Chairman, you will find it is not the mining companies which find the gold, the silver, the lead, the zinc, the molybdenum. It is the hard-bitten character who may have a grizzly bear or a black bear out there breathing down his neck when he bends down to check a rock. He is the one who makes the majority of discoveries for mining companies. He is the one guy in the whole industry who has been totally ignored, and it is time he got his fair share.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, my interjection in this debate will, I assure hon. members, be very brief, but I was inspired, shall I say, to speak by what the hon. member for Spadina said this afternoon. I think there are a couple of points that should be made in order to set the record straight. Having listened to that hon. member, I can understand, if his

philosophy is that of the former government's, why the country fell into the economic mess in which indeed it did.
There is no suggestion in this legislation, I submit, that any taxpayer in Canada is going to have a tax free income, at least not if he uses it for his own personal benefit. Under the clause we are discussing there is no such thing as a tax free income in any case. The essence of it is that one of those companies that are incorporated for convenience, as has been suggested, or for the more efficient operation of a professional business, can attract for the chief shareholder a tax which is less than he would have to pay if he were receiving that money as an individual and putting it into his pocket in a form in which he could go out next day and buy a new car or take a holiday or spend it on various consumer products.
The effect of the changes that have been proposed in this clause, as I understand them, is that it would encourage Canadians who earn money to use it as an investment fund. Surely that is what the kind of economy we have, is all about. Unfortunately, the people who have their tax deducted at source are not the entrepreneurs in this country, and it is, after all, entrepreneurs who create jobs and who make work.
What this change in the tax law will permit is that a person who had an income which is larger than he may need to use in that particular year for his own personal comfort may delay paying income tax on that income for some time so that he can use it for other purposes. He may not want to invest his money in a pension fund, which may well have international investments; he may not want to invest his money in exploration; he may prefer to invest his money in his own community, in a local shop, a local enterprise, or a fish processing plant, as he might want to do in my riding, or a fishing vessel.
These provisions establishing this classification within the Income Tax Act will permit the high income doctor, the dentist or the lawyer, to establish such a company and to use that money before paying tax on it to encourage industry and enterprise in his own community. Clearly it gives recognition to the fact that some of these professional people have a shorter earning lifetime than a great many other people in our society. This provision gives them an opportunity to spread their tax. Certainly there is no suggestion, and no wish on my part as one of the members supporting this legislation, that it should provide a free ride for anybody or that it should permit them to permanently avoid paying tax. It would give them an opportunity to spread the tax. It would inspire them to generate jobs and provide opportunities in their communities. That is what I want to see and I would be happy if we would get on with it.
Mr. Chairman, I have a question for the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member for South West Nova accept a question from the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount?

Yes, Mr. Chairman.
November 1, 1979

Mr. Chairman, some of the sentiments the hon. member has expressed are, I think, very desirable, but my question is this: What distinction does he make between a lawyer and an accountant, for example, who is entitled to incorporate his practice and therefore benefit from this substantial deferment, as opposed to an employed lawyer or accountant in the same income range who is not entitled to it and must pay his tax immediately, and therefore does not have the advantage of being able to invest in a shop, a fishing trawler, or what have you, but must immediately turn over his savings, to the revenue authorities? What justification does the hon. member see for that distinction between an employed professional and an independent professional?

The hon. member raises a very difficult question. The only real differential, or substantial differential, that I could cite would be that the self-employed individual is, in fact, an entrepreneur. He is the guy who, in a great many cases, I suspect, is operating in rural areas in this country as opposed to metropolitan areas. He is employing people, purchasing office equipment or setting up a practice on his own and taking, perhaps, all the risks that are normally attributed to an entrepreneur, whereas the employed professional is not doing that. However, I would assume under this legislation that when the employed professional becomes a partner in a professional association which is employing him, he would no doubt be able to take advantage of the same provisions.
Mr. Chairman, 1 have another question for the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I find it difficult to allow the hon. member to put another question, it would be unfair to other members. The hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount will have a chance to come back with questions later.

Mr. Chairman, 1 have listened with some interest in the last hour or so to comments coming from both sides of the House, particularly to the anecdotes of the hon. member for Kootenay West about prospectors and the difficulties they have. I come from a riding where, as I mulled over in my mind all the different communities, 1 realized there are a number of communities which do not have a doctor, a dentist, a chiropractor or an accountant, communities like Atlin or Port Simpson and other places along the coast. While everyone was talking about people with incomes of $30,000, $40,000, $50,000 or $100,000 a year, we have areas in this country where, in some communities, there is unemployment of 30 per cent or more, and in some cases up to 50 per cent. We have heard talk about communities where part of the taxation base of this country is being set aside in order to make the lives of the well to do somewhat more plush.
When we talk about these individuals and professional groups, we should realize the fact that they are not really creators of capital. What in fact they do is either get capital from the state or get it from individuals within the community, and they get a substantial slice of capital in the communities in which they operate. 1 do not claim that a lot of them do not
Income Tax Act
put that money to use within that community, but I think a great deal of that capital is used for investment in order to create more capital for them as individuals, capital which does not go directly to the community.
In looking at the bill in relation to small business, the government in the past six months has given a substantial slap in the face to small business in this country with the ever-increasing interest rates. To date all we have had is a preliminary statement from the hon. member for Capilano, who has said there will be some increase in capital through the Federal Development Business Bank.
The problems created in this country by capital being taken out of the economy and put in the hands of a limited number of individuals who do not put it into small businesses which employ people over a period of time are very extensive. They are problems to which the government does not put its mind. This brings me to the core of my point, that in looking at this very small group we must necessarily take into account other skilled groups. I know the hon. member for Kootenay West indicated that the chiropractors of this country have not lobbied actively to be included in this special taxation, but we must look at it from the point of view of the government dealing with this issue. They have been chosen, for one reason or another, as a lobby group above and beyond steelworkers, paperworkers or fishermen. A lot of individuals who work in our economy certainly deserve some tax break. They carry the real burdens, for example, of the House of Commons and everything else in the country. An ever increasing burden is being placed upon those individuals.
The amount of capital at year end which professional individuals are allowed to retain already is very high. Doctors, dentists and accountants are highly advantaged individuals. What do they do with their capital? What advantages do these individuals have in the community? Generally they own their own homes because they have had enough capital coming in over the years to do so. They are well educated. They are capable of putting their children through university. At a time when there are many unemployed, disadvantaged, handicapped and people living on fixed incomes, why should the government continue to push for the very select high income groups, be they oil company executives, doctors or anything else? The answer is fairly obvious. The government has chosen a specific lobby group for some reason or other. Perhaps there is a likely prospect that they will gain voters or some other thing.
The small business question has not been addressed by this bill in any way. Why is there no attempt to deal actively with interest rates which now affect the cash flow of small businesses and their ability to carry ongoing stock or expand in any way? Yet capital is being given directly into the hands of individuals who will not turn it over into the economy with a domino effect. Making more capital available to entrepreneurs in the forest and mining industries perhaps would be more appropriate if there was a direct tag on it relating to job creation or some affirmative process.

November 1, 1979
Income Tax Act
During the same period of time we are looking at recent cuts in the unemployment insurance program. In my riding individuals involved in fish processing had very limited work opportunity this year. Many of them did not work long enough to be eligible for unemployment insurance. The government seems to sit idly by as if someone who earned $3,000 can make it through the rest of the year, and hands out 10 per cent or 15 per cent to people in the $30,000 to $100,000 bracket. Certainly this is a matter the public should take into account the next time they go to the polls.
1 have one question for the parliamentary secretary. Exactly how many individuals are eligible under this program? The previous speaker wanted to know how much capital was involved, but I should like to know how many individuals are affected by this? 1 am sure that information is readily available.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very short. 1 have just come from a committee meeting where the estimates of the Department of Finance were being discussed. There was no one present at the meeting to give us direction in terms of policy on this matter. I am sitting in the House now and I see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance is alone. This is no reflection on him as I am sure he is very able, perhaps a good deal more able than the minister, but the minister is not in town when we are considering this very important tax bill, Bill C-17. As a matter of fact, I saw notice of a speech which the Minister of Finance was to release at 1.00 p.m. eastern standard time on November 1, 1979 to the Empire Club of Toronto. When we are in the middle of such an important debate, and the estimates of this particular department are before committee, surely the minister and the parliamentary secretary should be here. The choice should not be between this Parliament-the House of Commons and its committees-and the Empire Club. The choice should be very, very clear: the minister should be here.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso raised the question of the presence or non-presence of the minister in the House for the proceedings of the Committee of the Whole. He received an answer in part from the House leader. If 1 had been provided with an opportunity, my first comments this afternoon would at least have given partial reassurance to the hon. member in that the minister intends, if transportation facilities work effectively, to be here at eight o'clock tonight. It is unfortunate that 1 have to make such a comment so late in the day. I give the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan that assurance.
A great many questions have been raised to which I should like to respond as fully as 1 can. I should like to begin by dealing with some of the questions of principle and broad dimension raised by the hon. member for Broadview-Green-wood and the hon. member for Spadina. I should like to follow those remarks by responding to specific questions raised by the hon. member for Dauphin, the hon. member for Jonquiere and

the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount, and if 1 can, the hon. member for Skcena. 1 am not sure I will have a number of answers available for the hon. member.
A great many of the comments 1 have heard this afternoon seem to be based upon serious misconceptions, not only regarding what existed but what is proposed by this clause in the bill. Let me review the situation.
Up to the time of the proposals in Bill C-32 of the last session of the last Parliament, the people being dealt with in this bill had the advantage of a small business or Canadian privately controlled corporation tax provision. It was a matter of deliberate policy of the preceding government which was supported on all sides, or at least by most of the members of the preceding House, and perhaps present members. It gave and gives a tax advantage to such corporations, a deliberate tax advantage. The persons who drew that legislation in the first place did not intend that it should apply to the particular persons with whom this present clause deals. Therefore, this present clause does not give an advantage; it takes an advantage away, one which perhaps was given inadvertently.
The proposal in the budget of last November was that particular taxpayers, people providing personal services, if incorporated, could revert to the standard position of a public corporation. In other words, they would be subject to tax approaching 50 per cent depending on the province in which they were resident. This proposal is a modification of that in two ways. It adds two professions, chiropractors and veterinarians, to the list of non-qualifying businesses. It attempts not to make incorporation prohibitive but to make it a neutral act. There are sound reasons for not making corporations prohibitive.
May 1 call it five o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
