subsubtopic: REPORT ON FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING CROWN CORPORATION FOR FORESTRY RESEARCH
speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of the latest report on the feasibility of establishing a Crown corporation or other body to carry out forestry research.
He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should start my remarks by explaining my interest in the subject. One or two people have asked me why I put such a motion on the order paper. It relates, of course, to the presence in my constituency of Macdonald College, which is the agricultural college of McGill University. In that college there is an active forestry division. Having explained that, let me speak to the subject.
I requested the production of documents following remarks made in the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on February 22 of this year by the then minister of the environment, Mr. Marchand, who was discussing the Forestry Development and Research Act and emphasizing the need for a national forestry policy. He stated that a "study will be completed and presented to the Canadian Council of Resource Environment Ministers in June", which was June of this year. He then went on to say that changes will be made as necessary and that the previous government was working toward a national forestry policy.
From the remarks of the opposition representative at that time, the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon), now in the government benches, the impression was left that he was interested from a national point of view. He stated soon after the remarks of the minister that this was a significant federal concern.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to say a few introductory words about the forest industry in Canada. A monthly letter of the Royal Bank of Canada came to my attention just today, as a matter of fact it was in the mail, the heading of which is quite appropriate. Under the heading of "The Forest and the Trees" it states:
Forestry Research
Canada's forest is by far its greatest source of national wealth. But we have been using it up faster than it can grow back into good shape.
Certainly the Canadian forest products industry has grown into Canada's largest industry by far. Its total shipments are now in the order of $13 billion a year. Mills producing pulp, paper, veneer, plywood, box boards and other wood-based products have proliferated across the country. All Canadians have a share in this industry since over 90 per cent of our forests are owned either by the federal or various provincial governments. This can be estimated as something in the order of more than 20 acres of productive forest land for every man, woman and child. Some 800 million acres are classified in Canada as productive forests.
Though there are many square miles of forest, much are too far north to be economically usable. Though there are also numerous stretches of forest in the south, they are in hopelessly substandard shape. There is some desire expressed, often enough by the Canadian Forestry Association, to improve the situation. The association has stated:
Inadequate attention to forest regeneration is responsible for restricting expansion possibilities in some regions, has reduced unemployment in others, and will result in a continuing decline in future forest-based jobs and revenues.
Our forest industry in Canada employs some 300,000 persons directly, and probably more than twice that number in associated work. The salaries of those 300,000 directly employed exceed some $4 billion per year. While Canada's share of the world's export market has been falling and is now less than 20 per cent, forest products still count for well over $8 billion per annum of our export market; in fact, far more than fishing, agriculture, mining and fuels. About two million acres of forest land are cut in Canada every year, but not a single province is able to claim an adequate regeneration of these areas that have been cut, plus those areas being lost to natural disasters. In fact, the backlog of forest regeneration attributable to all causes such as harvest, natural catastrophe and human activity is now in excess of 60 million acres.
Mr. F. L. C. Reed, one of the nation's leading forestry consultants, stated in a recent report for the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association:
A more intensive program of forest management is imperative if market opportunities are to be realized and emerging timber deficits offset.
Certainly every province has its tree nurseries and its reforestation programs. Canada ranks high among the nations of the world in forestry research. The problem is not one of the lack of technology or good intentions, it is simply that not enough is being done. It will take a deliberate commitment on the part of government, industry and, indeed, the public at large to ensure that our forests meet our future needs. One in ten Canadian workers directly or indirectly owes his livelihood to the forestry industry.
This is why 1 asked for these documents, and I have been told that they do not exist. I state simply that it is unfortunate the present government has not seen fit either to pursue the direction of the former government in trying to establish a national forestry policy, or to indicate its willingness through forestry research to at least assist in stimulating the provinces

November 1, 1979
Forestry Research
to ensure that there is adequate regeneration of our forestry industry.
I am well aware that the attitude of the present government is to give more power to the provinces. We have seen what has happened. Not one province is maintaining its position. The situation calls for some leadership at the federal level, and this is the reason I expressed my desire to see these documents. At this point I can only express my disappointment over the government's statement that such documents do not exist.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING CROWN CORPORATION FOR FORESTRY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) has moved for the production of papers on the privatization of the forestry research industry in Canada or, at least, the feasibility of a study with respect to the incorporation of forestry research under the purview of a Crown corporation. It was earlier thought that the hon. member was referring to studies that were conducted late last year with respect to the privatization of forest products research. However, this afternoon the hon. member has specifically mentioned a report which was concluded in 1979. The minister has stated categorically that he was not aware-nor am I aware, and it is our information that the department is not aware-of such a study being available at this time.
I do not have to elaborate on the privatization of the two laboratories because they were discussed at some length in this House last year. A new corporation was formed to assume the financial management responsibilities for the programs of forest product laboratories. The now non-profit corporation called Forintek, although it is experiencing some of the difficulties inherent in a change such as this, is proving successful in fulfilling its mandate to carry out the forest products research.
As 1 said before, forestry research is much more than research involved in making better forest products. It is much broader and far more complicated. It deals with how trees become established, grow and die. It deals with where they grow, what kills them and even the influence these trees have on the entire ecosystem. This research is undertaken by the federal government, some provincial governments, universities and the private sector. The Canadian forestry service, which is the federal research arm, has research establishments across the country and acts in close concert with the other interested bodies in the forestry sector.
Canada is known the world over as a forest nation. In fact, more than two thirds of our land areas is covered with trees and 84 per cent of the country is forest or wild land. As the hon. member has stated, some 300,000 people are directly employed in our forest industries. Another 700,000 are employed in secondary manufacturing and service industries which also depend on the forests. This adds up to a million people, or 11 per cent of our labour force. Everyone knows that forest products are among our most important exports. In fact, they account for almost 20 per cent of our total export trade.
[Mr. Herbert.)
Last year, the net contribution of the forest industries to Canada's balance of payments was $8.4 billion, $1 billion more than the combined contribution of fisheries, agriculture, mining and fuels.
For a country like Canada which depends so heavily on its export trade, this is a vital contribution to economic survival. And today, especially when we are all so concerned with Canada s economic health, we simply do not dare ignore the importance of our forests. Within 20 years forests will provide not only the traditional lumber, pulp and paper products but a multitude of sophisticated chemicals and up to 8 per cent of Canada s primary energy demand. Conservative estimates suggest that by the year 2000, direct employment in the forest industries will increase by 100,000 people or 25 per cent, the value of wood exports will double, while the total value added in 1978 dollars will rise from $9 billion to $18.7 billion.
The importance of our forests goes far beyond trade balances, or employment and production figures. It goes beyond anything we can measure so conveniently, for besides providing raw material for industry, our forests provide us with many other benefits. For example, they protect our watersheds from erosion. They stabilize stream flow and act as reservoirs for water from snow and rain, thereby reducing the hazards of flooding and drought. They also provide the basic backdrop to a related $3 billion outdoor recreation industry.
In the boreal forest region, which comprises so much of Canada's forest resource, growth rates of natural stands average little more than 21 cubic feet per acre per year. In the more productive coniferous forests of the west coast, growth rates of 80 to 90 cubic feet per acre per year occur. These growth rates, remember, are for natural unmanaged stands. Given simple management these rates could be doubled, and if intensive management is practised in the more productive areas, they could be tripled.
Impressive though these facts may be, the state of the nation's forests is not good. Although Canada is cutting only about 75 per cent of its annual allowable cut, much less than half of the apparent reserve timber is economically accessible. British Columbia has half of Canada's volume of standing timber, but even there the installed capacity of the coastal forest industry could more than utilize its present allowable cut. Most of the reserve timber on the north coast is currently inoperable and similar situations exist in various parts of the interior.
The prairie provinces have a surplus of wood, but much of it is too remote. In Ontario, the productive forest available for wood production has dropped by reason of other demands from 105 to 65 million acres during the past 10 to 15 years. Shortages will occur in the Thunder Bay region and the province will have difficulty in reaching the relatively modest target of nine million cunits annually on its 56 million acres of Crown forest land by the year 2020. Quebec has a theoretical surplus of wood, but much of it is in remote areas where harvesting costs are high. Many local shortages are occurring, especially for sawlogs. In general we are not making the best use of the inherent productivity of Canada's forest resource
November 1, 1979

base. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are actually experiencing deficits in softwood supply. The existing industry in New Brunswick could utilize 25 per cent more wood than can be produced on a sustained yield basis under existing standards of management.
How did we get ourselves into this mess? It is difficult to point the finger of blame at anyone. When North America was first settled, timber was regarded as a stock of wealth to be exploited and transformed into useful and saleable products. It was viewed no differently than were deposits of metals, minerals, coal and oil. Indeed, like these resources, much of the virgin timber was put there by nature over a period of centuries.
Had man been involved in the growing of forests, he would have put a different value on those trees. Society and the industry itself have long thought that, unlike minerals and fossil fuels, the forest resource is renewable. So it is, but there are many degrees of renewability. Left to herself, nature will renew forest crops, but in her own time, with her own choice of species and at her own rate of stocking. That could only be established by nature. If man is not satisfied with this arrangement, he can spend time and money to grow timber crops more to his liking, but these crops are no longer cost-free.
Until recently in Canada we limited our investment in timber crops to paying for protection. The situation facing us now is similar to that which gave rise to agriculture. Nomadic peoples depended on nature to provide game for them and forage for their animals. Such a way of life provided a livelihood for a small population that was forced to harvest nature's bounty over a large area. 'Agricultural practice showed that crops could be grown and harvested at less cost than wild crops could be harvested alone. With hindsight, we could demonstrate that growing and harvesting timberland close to the mills would frequently have been cheaper than harvesting more distant, variable and scattered natural stands of timber.
In the long run, the only answer is more effective forest protection and reforestation, combined with silvicultural treatments to increase the growth rate of the existing forests. More intensive management could double the yield of much of our forest land.
In 1977, spending from all sources was less than $60 million for reforesting and tending our forests. This year it will be some $200 million. Even this amounts to only half what the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers- CCREM-estimates is needed.
The Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers has been studying forest policy for several years. Last June at Kelowna, ministers reached a broad measure of agreement on a general forest policy statement. This included eleven policy principles, among which are: first, pre-eminent provincial jurisdiction over its own forest land; second, the need for compatible federal and provincial policies affecting the resource industry; third, stability of rural employment and
Forestry Research
communities; fourth, maintenance of the productivity of forest land; fifth, multiple use management of forest land; sixth, environmental protection; and seventh, priority for research.
These may sound like motherhood statements, but they are much more than we have ever had before. The ministers have agreed to meet again in Toronto in January to see what concrete measures we can take to implement the recommendations.
What is largely unappreciated, Mr. Speaker, perhaps because confrontation and conflict get most of the headlines, is the major role that co-operation between government agencies at different levels has long played in the management of our forests. Under the terms of confederation, the provinces own almost all the forest land within their boundaries and are therefore responsible for management of 90 per cent of Canada's productive forest. Nevertheless, the federal government is heavily involved in many policies and activities critical to their wise management. These include monetary policy, regional development, industrial efficiency, research and development, tariffs and trade, transportation and so on.
Progress in achieving greater understanding of the complexities of forest ecology so that improved ways can be found for making the forests more productive and their management more efficient depends on co-operation between the scientists and foresters studying these problems. There are some outstanding examples.
Consider that notorious pest, the spruce budworm. Since 1909 this insect has killed nearly 300 million cunits of timber in eastern Canada and has caused loss in the growth of trees that survived their attacks. The current epidemic covers roughly 150 million acres of spruce fir forest in eastern North America and extends from western Ontario to the Atlantic provinces.
This very serious problem demands a combined effort to solve. In fact, an international effort is required because of an agreement signed in August, 1977, to develop a joint Canada-United States spruce budworm research and development program. The main aim of this co-operation is to find better ways of controlling this major forest pest common to both countries.
The two countries are concentrating their efforts on improvements in such areas as monitoring budworm population levels and the development of better, more environmentally acceptable control techniques. Activities under the agreement include joint publication of results, exchanges of scientists and other specialists in the industry, exchange of biological material and equipment, and the establishment of joint ventures such as data and information pools.
The spruce budworm has been around for a long time. It is native to Canada. There have been at least seven major outbreaks in eastern Canada in the past 200 years, each covering millions of acres. The seriousness of this natural harvest, if one can call letting the budworm eat millions of trees a "natural harvest", has become much more grave in present times. The budworm is now competing with man for trees, trees, I might add, which we need for maintaining the

November 1, 1979
Forestry Research
economic life of Canada. Even if the budworm does not kill all the trees in a stand, its destructive force greatly increases the cost of using the remaining trees. We simply cannot afford to sit back and let the budworm eat itself out of house, home and trees and then slowly starve to death.
The main control method that has been used since 1952 to contain the budworm has been to spray the infected forests with chemical insecticides. The limitations of this technique are recognized and I would like to say something later about progress in biological controls. But just consider for a moment the economics of this situation.
In New Brunswick the protection program up to 1976 cost about $95 million. But this protection has allowed for a doubling of the forest industry's capacity; it increased the value of shipments by $4.7 billion and added value by $2.7 billion, wages by $889 million. Those are impressive benefits for a small province and the forests of New Brunswick, although not as healthy as all would like to see, are likely to stay green and alive.
It is clear, then, that a serious threat such as the budworm to the forest resource is a potential threat to the economy of this country.
Public reaction to the spraying program has been prominent at all times. Annual spraying of 10 to 20 million acres in eastern North America will probably be necessary during the next few years. However, please remember that the decision to spray or not spray is a provincial decision based on the best facts available. It is interesting to note that forest spray technology has improved tremendously in the last decades. Smaller and smaller dosages are being applied more effectively. Even the small dosages of insecticides of around three ounces per acre represent a total application of 2,000 tons of highly toxic biocide for a 20 million acre spray area. Doubts about hidden environmental effects are bound to trouble many people.
After several years of annual use of insecticides on a large scale, there has been no measured loss of other resources, nor any acceptable reduction in environmental integrity. The problem is still that large scale long-term spraying may have a small influence that could eventually compound into larger environmental results.
In a policy statement last year, the minister said that although some infested areas may require special pest control practices, it is known that pesticides may have long-term effects on other resources in the environment. Therefore, it is federal policy to minimize the use of spraying and actively support research into alternative control strategies, including biological control.
One could go on, Mr. Speaker, and cite other examples which demonstrate that the complexities of modern forest management demand close co-operation between government agencies and industry.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING CROWN CORPORATION FOR FORESTRY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for bringing forward this motion this afternoon on the production of papers relating to the forest industry. I appreciate this very much. Not only is it timely, but it gives me an opportunity to underline in the House the importance of the forest industry to the economy and Canadians generally.
During this afternoon's question period, I had a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. de Cotret). Of course, he does not have the privilege of responding to questions in the House because he is in the other place. Therefore, I asked the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) about the government's position on the importance of planning and the future of the forest industry in Canada. I learned he had nothing to say about this important industry. He responded that he would take it as notice, that he would find out something about the forest industry in Canada and get back to the House. I find it rather strange for a member of the cabinet not to be able to answer on the importance of the forest industry on funds for expansion, and the construction of new pulp and paper mills in Canada. Hon. members will agree on the importance of this subject to Canadians. This is borne out by the fact that over one quarter of our exports is related directly or indirectly to wood products.
As I say, I am pleased the hon. member has brought forward this motion for the production of papers this afternoon. I represent a constituency in New Brunswick. Seventy-five per cent of that province is inundated with forest products.
I think I am making my case as to the importance to my area, the Atlantic region, and indeed to all of Canada of this most important subject.
The government did not consider this matter in its deliberations when preparing the throne speech. There is no mention of or reference to the government's position regarding plans for research and development of the resource industry, its position on exports, or its disposition on financing to assist the pulp and paper industry. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and his advisers will want to look seriously at putting this all important subject under the purview of a specific minister in the cabinet who will answer to this House and ensure that this important industry is protected in the manner it should be. There was no reference to this in the Speech from the Throne.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is nowhere near this House. We cannot pose questions to him or receive responses as we should. This minister ran in the last election, and was defeated. He now sits as a Senator and controls this all-important portfolio. Apparently he is the chief adviser to the government on economic development in this country, with specific reference to industry, trade and commerce, which is all encompassing. This brings me to the topic we are discussing today, the forest industry.
November 1, 1979

I thought the Minister of State for International Trade would have taken this subject to heart, concerned himself, and been briefed. I thought he would have discussed this with his colleague in the other place, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He could have at least apprised himself of the status of this important subject.
1 have already made the case as to the importance of this. 1 do not think much has to be said. It speaks for itself. It involves the economy, employment, and is of importance to Canadians in the process of development of this rich natural resource. What do we have from the government which whiles away its time talking about the past,-what this minister did, what that minister did, and what that minister did not do? We all know that leading up to May 22 they were telling Canadians they were ready and wanted to govern. However, since that time all we have heard is that it is the other fellows' fault, that they did it last year. When is this government going to take a serious look at accepting its responsibility to govern, if that is what it wants to do?
I come to the question before us today with regard to the forest industry in Canada. I make a plea to the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues to concern themselves seriously with the development of the forest industry in Canada. How can they justify their position and their operations on a day to day basis while totally ignoring the paper industry?
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) in his committee responsibilities is responsible for the environment. Naturally he is concerned with forestry as well. He debates and discusses with members of that committee what can be done to develop an over-all strategy for the future of the forestry industry in Canada. We will be hearing more from the hon. member for Davenport as he carries out his duties with respect to the environment. He will obviously be concerned with the protection of this all-important resource.
This leads me to the question of reforestation. In recent years many private corporations have taken the positive decision to accept their responsibility and direct funds to reforestation. For years we have been preaching that they cannot continue to rape our forests without giving some thought to the future and the replenishment of this resource.
In the region I represent there are many companies such as the Irving interests, Rosay Pulp and Paper, New Brunswick International Paper, CIP, Fraser companies and Bathurst Consolidated. They have taken this matter seriously in recent years. It is not only a question of discussion. They have put their money where their mouth is, and taken decisions to allot funds, millions of dollars for silva culture, nurseries, and the restoration of this important product.
I fail to understand how a government which has only recently come to office can continue to be as negligent as it is by not specifically identifying a minister as being responsible for this natural resource. I am not talking only about one region of the country. This concerns many regions from coast to coast. We all know the importance of the forest industry to
Forestry Research
British Columbia. We know its importance to Quebec and to the maritime provinces.
The government has talked about a merchant marine fleet, it has referred to a few other pale, weak topics in the document known as the Speech from the Throne. Why did ministers not avail themselves of the opportunity to say something about the forest industry, letting us know what their plans are, what their thinking is on this subject? But, no. They missed this glorious opportunity and now, to add insult to injury, we discover from personal experience that it is very hard to find ministers who are able to reply to our questions on this subject.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. de Cotret) is not in this chamber to answer questions, and when we put questions to the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) we find he is not sure of the position-he has to look into the matter and find out. No one objected to giving members opposite a few months, a honeymoon period, in which they could find out how the system ticks, where their offices are located, and who is responsible for what. But here we are, on November 1, 1979, getting ready to go into the eighties with a minority government which has not yet been able to sort these things out. It is a serious situation, and a serious problem faces all Canadians because every Canadian is affected directly or indirectly by this industry.
I am taking this opportunity to go on record as making a plea to the government to consider this important topic and develop its strategy, and announce whatever plans they may be able to agree upon. I refer particularly to the minister responsible for the environment, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cros-bie), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), the Minister of State for International Trade, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey), and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander). All these ministers have responsibility, directly or indirectly, to Canadians who are affected by this industry whether they work in the forests, in the cutting operation, whether they are employed in the mills or whether they are affected as users or consumers of the finished product.
The government should remember, too, that it is not only the forest product we are talking about. We are talking about people. We say we want to act on the people's behalf and it is people we should primarily be concerned about. Why does the government not express some form of good faith by designating a minister who is to be responsible for forestry? speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at five o'clock, p.m., clause 38 of the bill was under consideration and the hon. member for York East had the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at five o'clock, I was in the midst of beginning a response to some of the comments and questions made by several hon. members on clause 38. In particular I was beginning to respond to some of the points raised by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood and the hon. member for Spadina. 1 had suggested that it was possible some of their comments, particularly the ones of the hon. member for Spadina, were based on some misconception as to what this clause was intended to accomplish and what in fact it said.
This clause is to correct an advantage which had been given unexpectedly by the small business preferred tax rate. When the provision was drawn in earlier legislation, I am sure it was not intended to cover what are now proposed to be declared non-qualifying corporations. The special tax privilege which exists and which has widespread support, is designed to encourage small Canadian businesses. It was not designed to encourage the kinds of businesses which quite properly under the law t>egan to take advantage of the preferred rate and which are now removed from that advantage by this proposed legislation.
Hon. members will recall that the treatment to be accorded to these businesses in the budget proposals of the former minister of finance would have placed a penalty on incorporation for personal services covered in this proposal, because it would have found them paying a greater tax under the general public corporation rules than the proposal now before the House.
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood asked me yesterday and today what is meant by neutralization. This is what this clause is designed to do. It is designed to ensure that these non-qualifying businesses, by getting a 3316 per cent tax rate and having the normal gross-up and dividend tax credit treatment, will leave their owners in the same position as if they received the income directly in the first place, with one provision, that in fact the income is paid out fully in the form of dividends. If the income is not paid out fully in the form of dividends, as the hon. member for Saint Henri-Westmount has mentioned in particular, there is advantage to be gained by tax deferral. It is a limited advantage because, if the money not so paid out is invested and produces investment income, it incurs the 46 per cent to 50 per cent tax depending on what province one is in and not the 33!6 per cent tax.
While there can be some advantage in the deferral provision, it is likely to be a limited one. In general, moving from the 25 per cent rate accorded under the small business provision which these corporations now enjoy to the 33!6 per cent rate proposed, leaves their owners in exactly the same position as if they had paid themselves salaries directly. This is because by the route concerned they can pay a corporate tax, and then through grossing-up and receiving a dividend tax credit, if they are in a high enough tax bracket, they pay a personal tax. The sum total of the tax paid in the corporation and on the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Scott, Victoria-Haliburton).]
dividends received is the same as it would have been on a similar direct income amount.
That being the case, I find it hard to accept the statements suggested by the hon. member for Spadina who seemed to think that this was some kind of giveaway. In fact it is a kind of take-back which is designed to put these taxpayers in a non-privileged position as compared to the position they are in today. It is a take-back which does not impose an extra penalty that would deter such activities from taking place in incorporated form, because often there are very good non-tax reasons for doing so.
I should like to respond to some specific questions raised by hon. members. The hon. member for Dauphin inquired as to the effective date of this proposal. Generally speaking the effective date would be for the taxation year 1980 or one beginning in that year, as I understand it. In other words, the old provisions are in effect up to this moment.
The hon. member for Jonquiere informed us of some of the concerns of one of his constituents, a doctor. I would like to respond to the questions he raised. First of all, if I heard the concerns expressed correctly, his constituent was thinking in terms of what was proposed by the former government, in other words going into the same tax bracket as a public corporation and the positive disadvantage for incorporation that would imply.
His basic question was about these groups of people. I think I can do no better, sir, than to refer to a statement I have here which gives some of the reasons. I would preface this by saying that whatever division is drawn it is somewhat arbitrary. There are always going to be people on one side or other of the line about which one could argue. I think there are some very good reasons for the decision that has been taken.
The first point is that these professional groups by and large do not face the kind of business risks that are common to other businesses, including other areas of the service sector. The demand for services from these professionals is relatively inelastic, for obvious reasons. On the other hand, the demand for services such as those of engineers, architects and consultants, like those in most other businesses, is exceedingly sensitive to cyclical instability.
A second point is that these professional groups, especially doctors, lawyers, dentists and accountants, face much less competitive risk because the supply of their services is rigidly controlled through the existence of professional regulations and standards that make entry into the profession difficult, at least over the short and medium term.
Consultants, retailers, wholesalers, barbers, general insurance agents, manufacturers and so on face strong competition because of the ease with which new businesses can enter the field. In some cases these other concerns face strong competition from large multinational firms. It is no coincidence that bankruptcies among these professional groups are rare, whereas in the other groups they are a continuing conspicuous phenomenon.

In short, the mix of a relatively fixed demand for their services and restricted entry into their profession distinguishes these professionals from virtually all other businesses where the forces of competition operate in a way that greatly increases the element of risk.
A third major point is that because of the more limited element of risk, incorporation is not and has not been an essential element for the successful conduct of these professions. In fact, incorporation has been sought largely, if not exclusively, in the past for tax reasons. The' one province that allows professionals to incorporate does not permit limited liability. Other business sectors, including other personal services and other professions, have a history of incorporating which pre-dates the existence of favourable tax treatment, and that is explained by the need to protect shareholders from excessive financial risk.
Another point is that the element of providing special incentives for small businesses so as to permit them to become established, to grow and to eventually turn into large competitive domestic and international corporations and provide large numbers of jobs to Canadians, is not an aspect that applies to the professions mentioned. They will not be a main source of increasing growth in job opportunities. Other business sectors, including services, are where future growth and expansion will occur, either through small businesses growing into large businesses or through an increse in the number of small firms in those sectors.
The hon. member for Jonquiere may consider that some of these are very compelling reasons for the particular division that has been drawn, even though I am sure he and his constituent might argue about some activities at the boundaries.
The hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount raised some questions of principle about the tax. I am not sure that they can be fully met by the proposal before us, but I trust he will consider that the merits of this proposal outweigh any of the negatives which he feels may exist.
The hon. member is concerned about the principle of neutrality and equity as I think all of us are, and he raised a question about the value of the deferral privilege. 1 have already commented on that and I hope he considers that the qualification I have suggested as to the importance has some practical significance. He raised also the question of regional equity and pointed to the fact that only in some jurisdictions is incorporation permitted. That is indeed a fact, though it is not a static fact and it may change. I think it is reasonably fair to say that there are other instances where tax burden varies regionally because of legislative actions or regulations by other jurisdictions within the federation. There is no compelling and effective answer to his point, except to say that such imperfections exist, and probably are not too important unless they are major.
The hon. member for Skeena raised the question of how many individuals are affected by this proposal. I am sorry that I have not been able so far to obtain a number. I am told that
Income Tax Act
for the professionals there are very few, but for all categories involved there are a very few thousand entities affected.
I think those are the main questions that called for answers, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance has done a very credible job of defending the indefensible in terms of some of the points raised. I must say I do not understand the last comment the hon. member made when he suggested very few entities were affected. I am not sure in what context that was made, but perhaps he could clarify that in responding to a couple of points I would like to put to him.
There is some validity to the thesis the hon. member put forward, that what is being done is taking away something which existed rather than creating further tax inequities. The hon. member says we are moving to approximately 33 V5 per cent depending on the provincial jurisdiction and the incidence of tax in that jurisdiction as I read the statute, as opposed to say 25 per cent to which these groups would otherwise be entitled. The hon. member makes the point, as I understand it, that this provision was originally intended to permit the accumulation of capital in industries where future growth and future job expansion is anticipated. I understand all of those points quite well, but what I am troubled by is the fact that this still remains a very arbitrary provision in terms of singling out these particular professions for what the hon. member would now describe as less preferential treatment, if you like. In fact it is not preferential treatment as most of these professions at the moment are accorded no such treatment because they cannot incorporate.
I think I am correct in saying, certainly with regard to accountants and lawyers, that across this country for the most part, with the exception I believe in the case of Alberta, such incorporation is not permitted. Therefore I say the tax neutrality principle is really offended in a very major way because there are other industries today, admittedly growth industries such as management consulting firms, which are placed in exactly the same position, or should be regarded in the same way as law firms and accounting firms. As you know, most of our major management consulting firms in this country, or a large number of them, are affiliated with or are offshoots of our major accounting firms.
I am not really satisfied that we should put this definition in the act as to those specific professions that should benefit, or be prejudiced by, 33 W per cent rate. Talking about the limited advantage, I do not regard that as a limited advantage. When a professional in my jurisdiction is subject to 70 per cent income tax on personal income in excess of $60,000, I believe it is a year, as opposed to a position where he or she is subjected to an immediate 33'A per cent tax with an indefinite deferral until such time as dividends are paid up, particularly in a time of inflation, and it is hardly offset by the fact that the additional revenue which one receives on the tax savings will be taxed at 46 per cent.

If it were not a very substantial advantage, I suggest that we would not have this legislation before us and the government would have accepted Bill C-37 which was introduced last year. Obviously this bill is not intended to take the entire advantage which the government believes exists with respect to some of these corporations, and I cannot accept that as a valid position.
I am not trying to defend Bill C-37. I did not like its provisions either. I believe that this whole area is fraught with inequity and is basically a real "Rube Goldberg" type of legislation in terms of small business corporations. We now have 25 per cent rates, 33 per cent rates, and 46 per cent rates. We had different provisions with respect to dividend payouts. We have eight pages in the statute to cover this particular amendment.
I for one have always pushed for simplifying these statutes, and I find that this is not only offensive to the principles of tax neutrality but it is also offensive to the principles of tax simplification. Going beyond that, I find myself on the horns of a dilemma because I am really not quite sure what to tell the government to do with this provision. I am not sure basically how we should be looking at it at this stage of the proceedings in terms of how it can be improved. I can think of ways of improving subsection (/)(i) because, as I say, that is too limited. But as long as there is a recitation of people who benefit, somebody is always bound to be left out. That is why that particular kind of legislation is offensive in itself, just as the provision-and hon. members may be familiar with them-with regard to income averaging annuity contracts are limited to certain specific types of beneficiaries.
I have always felt that this is unfair because other people also have fluctuating incomes. Why should they not benefit from income averaging annuity contracts instead of only entertainers, writers, authors, musicians and so on. 1 am very concerned about enumerating this group and putting them into this special category. I also take issue with other arguments, but I do not see much point in doing so when the government is saying that these particular professions are not sensitive to cyclical instabilities. Obviously the government is not familiar with the situation of a lawyer in my province over the past few years whose specialty is seeking financing, or the government would take issue with that statement and say, "Yes, lawyers are subject to cyclical instability." Or if one were a member of the notarial profession, which 1 know is not covered in this list in Quebec, and basically dependent on real estate transactions, one may take the same point of view.
As a general statement, considering the climate in which we live, particularly in my province, I suggest that any of these professions are subject to cyclical instabilities, even in the dental and medical fields. I wonder if it would be possible some time in the course of these discussions to obtain a commitment from the Minister of Finance that he will take it upon himself to study this area in an attempt to come up with some better legislation than we have here and to come up with legislation which rationalizes the entire use of corporations, particularly in the small business sector, and corporations for use by professionals.

We are still subject legitimately to criticism by the whole range of wage earners in this country who receive no deferral. Once they have moved into the $15,000 a year bracket, they become subject to taxes in excess of 3396 per cent. I do not think that this is a fair provision, nor did I think that the original provision was fair. I think that we are grafting another provision onto this Income Tax Act which will result in further inequity and complication. I would very much welcome intervention by the Minister of Finance-perhaps it could be in his budget in November-to improve the Income Tax Act.
Frankly, I would like the improvements to be broader than just this one area, but this one area which has always troubled me, because in a country where there are such different jurisdictions and different vehicles, particularly in the corporate vehicle, it seems dreadfully unfair to me that a person's fundamental income should be subject to such great differences by virtue of a vehicle he selects, to do his business through, and that he is obliged to select, for example, in law, the partnership, where lawyers in Alberta can enjoy the enormous benefits which they already enjoy plus this income tax advantage which, on its face, creates a great disparity between the position of lawyers-and I cite lawyers because I am familiar with the profession-in the east and lawyers in the west.

Mr. Chairman, I am delighted that my earlier intervention and the interventions of my party have finally prompted the other party to move away from their slumber and attempt to come to grips with a very important provision of this bill. One of the ironic features of this debate is that there is not one member of the Liberal party, with the exception of the hon. member for Spadina who is no longer here, who is attempting to defend or even understand the provisions of Bill C-37. That party is not prepared to stand by a very important amendment to the Income Tax Act which it put forward a short 11 months ago. It is not prepared to indicate their support for it or for any of the arguments which are in writing and which are written at length in the bills which accompany the budget of November, 1978. Where is the Liberal party?

In his remarks, the hon. member for Jonquiere has referred to the problems of professionals without dealing with the fundamental issue, namely, the principles of justice within our tax system, and he has been unable to defend the policy of his colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, the former minister of finance.

Although I disagree with the implications of many of the things stated by the hon. member for Saint Henri-Westmount,
I learn something every time I listen to him. He too is not prepared to support the fundamental propositions laid out in Bill C-37. The hon. member could give no indication of what those propositions are other than calling virtually for a new Carter commission, a new look at the whole question of corporate income tax and its relationship to personal income
November 1, 1979

tax. I agree that that would be a good idea, but it does not address itself to this particular problem.
The hon. member has said that he does not know what to do about this particular measure, and he cannot give any positive recommendations as to what should be done about this particular provision which is before us. That is no surprise, though, because the hon. member for Saint Henri-Westmount is a Liberal. He cannot make up his mind whether he should support something which comes from the last Parliament or whether he should be against it.
He should get cloned like the financial critic.

1 would rather be cloned than well honed like the Minister of Finance. I believe that the basic principles which were put forward and which the parliamentary secretary attempted to defend have really not been answered. The first critical question is fairness-what tax lawyers call "equity". That question really has not been addressed. There has been much talk of tax neutrality, yet the minister has said in the statement accompanying this change that the effect of the measure will be to grant an advantage to those who incorporate over those who do not incorporate. I suggest to him that he has given no figures which would indicate the reverse. He has introduced no figures to indicate the contrary. There are no tables accompanying his proposals to indicate that there would not be a significant advantage to incorporating rather than not incorporating.
I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that if there were not this advantage, we would not be having this debate tonight. He knows perfectly well the only reason we are debating this is that those people who were affected by the changes recommended by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, were going to lose money over the proposition. It would have required them to start paying tax as if they were like other income earners. It is not simply that they would be employees; that is not what is being disputed. What is being disputed is that even those people who are self-employed would be paying tax at a higher rate than if they were allowed to incorporate.
I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that, for all the talk of tax neutrality, he knows perfectly well that were there not a significant advantage to this group of professionals in incorporating, we would not be here tonight debating the measure. It is only because the government proposes to give them that advantage over the measures proposed by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, that we are here tonight.
The first point the parliamentary secretary made was that nothing is given; something is being taken away. That is only true if you ignore the fact that the budget was presented in which certain propositions were put forward and in which certain facts were revealed to the Canadian public. If we pretend there was no November budget and if we pretend there had not been this powerful lobby mounted by the various professionals on the Parliament of Canada, if we pretend that those things had not taken place, then what the parliamentary
Income Tax Act
secretary says might be true. That is not what happened, however. We had a budget which presented a very coherent statement, which attempted to underline something of the clear abuse which had taken place as a result of court decisions and of behaviour in the market place.
Hon. members opposite who are interested in the market place know perfectly well what is going on out there. They know perfectly well that professionals who incorporate have a significant tax advantage over people who do not incorporate. They know perfectly well that people who can declare themselves to be self-employed have a significant tax advantage over people who are not self-employed. I suggest it is not possible for us to wipe away 11 months of history. It is not possible for us to wipe away a fact which has become evident, that there was an abuse in the system.
The government has admitted there was some kind of abuse because it has attempted to respond to the various court decisions outlined in my earlier remarks, by bringing in this new half-baked, hybrid measure. This hybrid measure creates a third category of incorporation, as if the Income Tax Act were not complicated enough and as if we did not have enough difficulty understanding the statute. The Conservative party has introduced yet another measure. I should like to point out to the minister and the parliamentary secretary that whatever the half-hearted nature of the Liberal proposal and the Liberal criticisms of this measure, our criticisms of it are quite clear; it is an offence to fairness and it is an offence to the simplicity and comprehensibility of the tax act.

I know the Liberal party is not interested in arguing about this, but I think it is a very important problem. I have a question to which I hope the minister will find the time and the ability to address himself at some point. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion perhaps will be able to deal with it as well. It is a very fundamental question. Is the investment tax credit working? It is a very substantial sum of money to be giving to corporations to invest in particular areas when two things are possible, and we do not have the information before us.
The first problem is that investment might have taken place in these areas in any event, in which case the expenditure of government money is completely unnecessary and provides a substantial benefit to companies which might well have taken the same decision in the absence of any incentive or movement by the government. It is very critical to ask whether this is the best way to be spending $130 million of government money in a particular year and how it compares with the direct expenditure of money. There are very few ways of controlling the credit compared with capital cost allowance. Even in comparison with capital cost allowance it strikes me as being an inefficient way to carry on in terms of tax expenditures.
Second, does this form of tax expenditure, which is designed not just to increase investment but to increase investment in particular regions of Canada, provide the government with an excuse for not carrying out direct expenditure?
[Mr. Rae.)
For example, in the field of scientific research and development the parliamentary secretary knows perfectly well that the private sector can decide, for reasons which may have nothing to do with the validity of the research and development expenditure, to do certain work in order to take advantage of a particular credit.
If you accept-and I know from the remarks made last night that the parliamentary secretary does not-the premise that there is such a thing as a tax expenditure and that it is just as much a form of public expenditure as direct expenditure, then I think the question for the taxpayers of Canada becomes, in research and development and in general investment: is this the best way to spend public money, and is this a very poor and inadequate substitute for the kind of direct expenditure in research and development and the kind of controlled and focused activity in terms of scientific research which really should be coming from the Government of Canada?

I am sure the hon. member agrees that one of the causes of a rather unsatisfactory economic performance in this country, particularly in the secondary sector, has been inadequate expenditure on research and development. Another cause, I think we can fairly say, is inadequate investment in general. There are some figures which may interest the hon. member.
In the opinion of many, an opinion I share, Canada has been deficient in research and development in terms of gross amount spent and in terms of who should do the research. Here are some interesting comparisons in terms of gross amounts: Canada, 1.1 per cent of its GNP; Germany, 2.1 per cent of its GNP; Japan, 1.7 per cent of its GNP; Switzerland, 2.2 per cent of its GNP, the United States, 2.3 per cent of its GNP.
The second aspect is how much of that research is performed by government and how much by industry, and the distinguishing characteristic of Canada is that not only have we had a lesser share of our GNP going into research, we have had a lesser share that has been put in by industry. Those two factors are both very significant in the kind of economic performance we have had in this country. Canada's percentage has been 40 per cent, which is very, very low by comparision with others such as Germany with 61 per cent, Switzerland with 77 per cent, Japan with 64 per cent, and the United States with 68 per cent.
One of the attractions of this particular proposal, and of its predecessors on which it is built, is that we are now beginning to encourage, as we did not for many years, research and development expenditure by industry, which, to my mind, is one of the best guarantees that R and D expenditures will be productive economically. That is the record of other industrial nations, and the hon. member has to produce some evidence unknown to me to counter it effectively.
The hon. member raises the question of whether these expenditures are effective-investment expenditures, investment tax credits, research tax credits. It is clear that they should be more effective than a comparable expenditure made directly by the government because, for one thing, there is a powerful multiplier effect. We give a tax credit of 5 per cent, 7

Another factor, and it arises out of experience 1 have had over many years in having to take part in decisions about investment expenditures and R and D expenditures, is that if an investment expenditure is going to cost you less or if an R and D expenditure is going to cost you less, and with the tax credit they do, then you spend money and it is worth your while to spend more, so you do spend more. I do not know if it would be possible for someone with the best sociological or economic weapons to go and determine how much more is spent collectively, but it is a matter of knowledge and logic that more is spent.

It is basically a question of cause and effect.
What we are talking about in this case is the effective expenditure of a very large amount of money in times of restraint, which could be used to alleviate some of the very serious social effects of the restraint program of the government in various areas of the country. I would like to look at this in terms of the regional development of the country because one of the prime aims of this clause, as set out in the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice last year, was that this measure would encourage development in certain designated areas of the country, specifically the four Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe part of Quebec. At that time my criticism of that particular provision was that we did not know whether it was going to encourage the level of investment in the Atlantic region.
It seems to me that businessmen who are contemplating an investment are going to look beyond the initial tax credits available to them in pursuing a certain investment, that the real factors affecting their decision as to whether or not to invest will be the over-all market conditions in a region, the availability of skilled labour, access to markets and so on, basic factors of the economy that this investment tax credit does nothing to solve. It has not been shown at all that providing this additional tax credit in certain areas of the country will do anything other than give a windfall to those individuals and corporations which have already, for other reasons, decided to invest in the particular region.
The business community in the Atlantic region is doubtful whether this particular provision has any effect on new construction or new investment in that region. I spoke with several individuals last year when this provision came out in the budget and the response I got was that the real problems in Atlantic Canada cannot be solved by some initial credit on investment in the region. The real problems are basic structural problems, fundamental problems in the relationship of the Atlantic region with the rest of Canada. It has nothing to do with the tax structure on investments. As I mentioned, the problems involve access to markets, the problems of a small local market, and the problem of the whole tariff structure which is geared historically to protect central Canadian industries to the detriment of the east and the west in the country.

In June of last year, when the then minister for science and technology announced a program with a proposal that by 1983 we would increase the percentage of gross national product spent in this country by the government, by universities and by private industries on research and development from the then 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent, he was criticized by the present Prime Minister, who spoke for the Conservative party, as well as by the spokesman for our party. Both of those hon. members said that even if we achieved that goal within the five-year period we would still be spending substantially less in terms of percentage of our gross national product for scientific research and development than is being spent by most industrialized countries in the world.
I am not going to go over the figures again, as the parliamentary secretary gave some of them a few moments ago. We said then that this was not enough and we called for increased efforts in government laboratories, in universities and in private industries in the field of research and development. We all agreed that what we should be aiming for was an expenditure of 2.5 per cent of gross national product, and sooner than 1983. That government, having set as its goal 1.5 per cent of the gross national product by 1983, proceeded within less than three months, because of the so-called need for restraint, to cut back on the money expended by the federal government, either through its own research laboratories or through grants to universities. It cut back on already woefully inadequate funds provided for scientific research.
This is not the time to talk about what is happening in government research laboratories operated by the National Research Council or by various departments concerned with agriculture, fisheries and forestry, but I want to deal with the situation in relation to the government's apparent belief that we can do better than we have in the past through some kind of greater concessions to the private sector of our economy.
Former governments, Liberal and Conservative, have tried to encourage private industry in this country to become involved in research and development. This government may believe that the carrots proffered to the private sector by former Liberal governments were not big enough or juicy enough. However, the former government did have programs. It had the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act, and it had a program for the advancement of industrial technology. Those programs did not succeed.
I was not here when my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood spoke, as I was attending a committee meeting, but I am certain he did not suggest that all research should be done by the government and monitored by government bureaucrats. No social democrat believes that. In spite of the fact that most members of the Conservative party are ignorant of the politics of government in other countries, there is a social democratic government in Germany and there was a social democratic government in Sweden for some 40 years. There have been social democratic governments in Great Britain, Norway, Belgium, Holland and Denmark. Most of

those countries are far ahead of Canada in terms of the efficiency of their industry.
In all those countries which have or have had social democratic governments, whose philosophy and policies are very much like those of the NDP, the private sector is alive and flourishing.
And trying to defeat the government.

And often trying to defeat the social democratic government, as is its right. There is a vast difference between those governments and this government or the former Liberal government. Those governments are not bound to wipe out or destroy the so-called free enterprise system. They accept the fundamental reality that we live in a mixed economy in which some parts of the economic system are owned and operated by the state and some have less government ownership or involvement. I think Sweden and Germany, which have or have had social democratic governments, have less public ownership than we have in Canada.
We have a tremendous amount of public ownership. We have a publicly-owned railway brought in by Liberal and Conservative governments, not by the social democrats. We have Air Canada, a publicly- owned air transport system, and in virtually every province we have publicly-owned electric power systems. 1 do not think there is a member in this House from any party who would suggest that was a mistake because we are getting electric power in Canada much cheaper than they are in the United States, for example, with privately-owned systems.
In the three prairie provinces we have publicly-owned telephone systems. In my province of Manitoba we have had a publicly-owned telephone system since 1909, brought into being by a Conservative premier, Sir Rodmond Roblin, whose name, I am sure, is known at least to some members in this House. We have a Conservative government in Alberta which not so long ago bought control of Pacific Western Airlines. When we advocate public ownership or government involvement in planning we are talking about hard reality and not some kind of unproven or untried theory.
Let me talk for a few minutes about this particular item. I have to assume that the parliamentary secretary suggested the government was going to make it easier and more profitable for industry in this country to spend money and effort on research and development, and that this is going to change the sorry state of research and development in this country. I do not want to go over the figures again, but among the industrial countries of the world Canada is, if not right at the bottom, close to the bottom in terms of the percentage of gross national product spent on scientific research and development. When we consider applied research we find that Canada is the last of eight industrial countries in terms of dollars devoted to industrial research and development.
Not only is the quantity of research and development conducted by industry in Canada very poor, but the quality
November 1, 1979

appears to be very poor. For example, it has been estimated that of the 110 significant innovations in the world since World War II-which covers a wide range of the science intensive industry including electronic components, pharmaceutical plastics, computers, among others-none were first developed in Canada. This survey covers the time period up to 1970, but recent data suggests that Canada still shows a poor performance. Of the 926 companies identified by Statistics Canada that were funding research and development in Canada during 1973, only $10.8 million was received from foreign countries as payment for patent licences and technological know-how. These same companies expended $75.6 million abroad for technology.
What are the reasons for the poor level of industrial research and development in Canada? There are two major reasons. First of all, most of Canadian industry which is Canadian-owned is in the resource extraction area, such as mining and forestry. Such industry requires very little research and development.
For example, in 1969 among the 14 nations belonging to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, Canada had the second lowest percentage of workers in the manufacturing area, 23 per cent, and it has gone down since. Ireland was the lowest at 20 per cent. West Germany was 28 per cent, the United Kingdom 36 per cent, and the United States 34 per cent. The second reason is that Canada has the highest degree of foreign ownership and control among the OECD countries. If one thinks of all the major industries-the automobile industry, the rubber industry, the electrical industry and so on-virtually all of them are almost completely dominated in this country by the multinational corporations.
The Toronto Star conducted a survey about one year ago. It contacted approximately 20 of the major industrial corporations in this country, General Motors, Ford, Westinghouse, Kodak, and Xerox among others. It knew how much business these companies had done in Canada, the amount of sales and so on. It asked each company how much research they did worldwide and how much research they did in Canada. The answers were very illuminating, and ran from no research and development for Kodak of Canada to virtually nothing for the automobile companies. That outlines the problems which this country faces and which this government is ignoring. These large multinational companies must do their fair share of research and development in Canada, and it must be comparable with their sales activity in Canada. There is no evidence that if we give them tax concessions they will do the job.
That brings me to small companies which employ a large number of people in this country. Small companies are usually Canadian-owned and are interested in going ahead. This system does not help small businesses because they must make a certain amount of money before they can take advantage of the tax benefits proposed in this bill. We need more than just a tax gimmick to get companies which operate in Canada to do research and development here. We need a much more aggressive and much more planned system, as well as a great deal
Income Tax Act
more government involvement in the form of consultations, co-operation and direction.
I had the opportunity recently to spend a couple of days in Japan. While there our group received a briefing by the Canadian ambassador to Japan. I want to say to the parliamentary secretary that his description of the role which the Japanese government plays in how the country will operate and how industry will be encouraged to expand to meet the needs of the domestic market and the international market so that Japanese workers will have jobs, was very broad.
Japan has a free enterprise system of government. The socialist party is not very strong there. Flowever, any resemblance between the free enterprise system of Japan and that of Canada is almost completely coincidental because there the free enterprise government plays a very active role. It meets on a day to day basis with companies, and it insists that what they do when these companies expand should help, not just the companies, but the Japanese people by providing better jobs and more efficient, technologically oriented industry. Until Canada can achieve that level of expertise, these tax concessions which are being proposed will not begin to meet our very serious failure to modernize and make Canadian industry competitive not only in the Canadian market but in the international market where we must get our share of sales if our unemployment figures are to remain low over the next ten years or 20 years.

subtopic: ENERGY-OIL PRICES-REQUEST GOVERNMENT ABANDON PLANS FOR FURTHER INCREASES
ENERGY-OIL PRICES-REQUEST GOVERNMENT ABANDON PLANS FOR FURTHER INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rules of this House give us only seven minutes to express a point of view at this time. It is difficult to control one's anger for seven minutes on the policy of this government with respect to oil and energy prices in particular. Yesterday the Economic Council of Canada released a review the French title of which is "The Burden of Inertia". I think one could hardly find a better description of this government, particularly with respect to its energy policy.
We have a government that does not listen to public opinion. We saw how this government does not take into account public opinion with respect to Petro-Canada. Not only do we have a deaf government, we now have before us a government which has grown mute when it comes to energy prices and oil prices in particular. The provinces have expressed very clear opinions-the province of Alberta, the province of Ontario. But the
November 1, 1979

Canadian public and this House have been unable to extract any information whatsoever from this government on the policy it intends to carry out with respect to oil prices. That is showing contempt for this House and the Canadian public. It is unacceptable that after being in power for more than five months the government should still be unable to say to this House what it is actually proposing to Canadians in terms of an oil price policy.
Yesterday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) appeared before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works and we were unable to get any information whatsoever from him. Even members sitting on the government side could not get any information at all from that minister. That completely withrawn approach of the government must be denounced, and I am sure, rejected, and considered unacceptable by Canadian public opinion. [English]
The irresponsible attitude of the present government concerning the matter of energy pricing, oil pricing in particular, is to be condemned. The province of Ontario and the province of Alberta have come out with clear statements on where they stand. This government will not tell the House and the Canadian public where it wants to take the people of Canada with regard to energy pricing, oil pricing in particular.
At the present time there is an agreement in existence with the provinces which provides for a $ 1 a barrel price increase in January. This would guarantee peace with regard to energy pricing until July 1, 1980. We now hear the government wants to dump this agreement and to tax the people even more by substantially increasing the price of oil. It wants to do this although we have an agreement that has been signed, sealed and delivered on this subject, with the province of Alberta.
This government only thinks about increasing the burden upon the Canadian public. We now have the highest interest rates in our history. Under this government we are heading toward the highest ever prices for oil and gas. According to what we can distinguish from this government's policy, every Canadian home owner and car driver will be taxed an additional $200 at least in the next year. That is over and above the additional cost that will be incurred because of the high interest rates this government has brought forward since taking office in early June.
These are steps that should be fought by all Canadians. They will be fought by the opposition both inside and outside this House. Our position is that we should not be chasing after international prices. That position was made quite clear in 1976 in our white paper on energy. Hon. members can find it on page 127 of our white paper on energy, it reads:
It is the federal government's objective to see domestic oil prices increase to a level sufficient to bring on new Canadian supplies. To the degree that this level is lower than international oil prices it is a differential for the benefit of Canadian consumers and Canadian producers, industrial and agricultural.
Let us have the price determined in Canada by Canadians for Canadians. Let us not slavishly follow a price set up by the
Adjournment Debate
international cartel which is called the OPEC countries. The attitude of the government in taking this country to international prices is one which will drive this country into a recession next winter and next year, in addition to the high interest rates being imposed on our citizens at this time. I urge the government to reconsider its course and to maintain the policy which the previous government set up, one of moderate and gradual increases in price and one where the highest level would be determined by the cost of finding and distributing new resources in Canada rather than being at the mercy of the OPEC countries.
