subtopic: ENERGY-OIL PRICES-REQUEST GOVERNMENT ABANDON PLANS FOR FURTHER INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would point out to the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) that we have had 11 years of inertia. We have seen the maritimes left totally dependent on foreign oil and gas; we have had a nation without an energy policy for 11 years-nothing under way though proven supplies were falling.
The government is working today on a national oil policy based on energy self-sufficiency. Oil self-sufficiency for Canada is essential. In order to achieve self-sufficiency we cannot continue to rely on foreign sources of oil over which we have no control as to the price charged or the quantities available. The government is now working with the provinces and the industry to establish a domestic price for oil which will provide incentives for, and cover the cost of, the production of new oil. Appropriate pricing can also contribute to reducing growth in demand. We cannot continue to expect that international supplies of oil will be available in quantities sufficient to meet rapid demand growth. We must plan to get through the next decade with more limited requirements.
Among many other important matters which are being discussed with the provinces to obtain agreement on an energy policy package are the implications of an energy price increase. These include the effects on home owners, car drivers, industry and so on. The macro-economic implications are also being studied by my department.
In his original question the hon. member referred to a communication from the provincial premiers following their meeting on October 23. They asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to re-establish the technical advisory committee on petroleum supply and demand and to improve formal communication between the provinces and the National Energy Board.
In reply to the premiers the minister noted that he was reviewing the current and prospective oil product supply situation and is likely to require reconvening the technical advisory committee, particularly in light of its tenuous legality. He also noted that the National Energy Board data is regularly reviewed with the provinces and that the next such review was scheduled for November 5. This government will shortly announce a Canadian energy package based on pricing for

November 1, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Canadians guaranteed to ensure energy self-sufficiency in Canada, by Canadians and for Canadians, by 1990.

subtopic: ENERGY-TANKER TRANSPORTATION OF CRUDE OIL ON WEST COAST
ENERGY-TANKER TRANSPORTATION OF CRUDE OIL ON WEST COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is in relation to Alaskan oil, and before I get too far along with it I would like to put a few quotations on the record. The dilemma with which this country is now faced is the result of an inheritance from the previous Liberal administration, and the difficulty is that the Alyeska line was built from the north slope down to Valdez, and tankers have been transiting down the British Columbia coast for the past two years. The Liberal administration did absolutely nothing in terms of dealing with either liability, jurisdiction, clean-ups or any of the ongoing difficulties which were arising at that time.
The Liberals simply brushed those off, and in speaking with the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) two weeks ago and questioning him in relation to the difficulties on the west coast and in relation to both the Foothills proposal and the northern tier proposal as well as the TransMountain proposal, I recognized that he has in fact inherited a very serious difficulty from the Liberal party.
I would like to quote first from the Thompson statement of proceedings from 1978, pages 62 and 63. In the first one he states very clearly in his testimony that "a dangerous situation now exists in the waters of southern British Columbia." That was in 1978. On page 63 he states:
Since an increasing amount of this traffic is originating from Valdez and travels along the entire outer coastline of British Columbia, in the middle of our fishing zone, this assessment must encompass a broad geographic region.
He was speaking in relation to environmental, social, navigational and safety aspects of the tankers which were already there. From a recently released environmental impact statement by Cecil Andrus, from pages 37 and 39 I quote as follows:
Presidential Executive Order 12114, signed January 4, 1979, exempts from detailed environmental analyses those portions of a major federal action which might have an effect on the environment of a foreign nation.
That is directed specifically at Canada. At page 39:
If a major oil spill occurred in the Strait of San Juan de Fuca, Port Angeles Harbour, or along the cross-sound pipeline route, it would affect marine resources, water quality, shorelines, shoreline structures, boats, and waterfowl over a wide area. Such an impact could also affect the Pacific coastline, the U.S.-Canadian shorelines of the Strait, and Puget Sound.
Further down on the page:
The cumulative effect of small chronic oil spills is expected to have more adverse impacts than an occasional major spill.
The point I wish to make in all of this-and there are further quotations I will give in a moment-is that the federal government has not given appropriate sanctions or studies in relation to tanker traffic which exists off the coast of British Columbia. The Prime Minister and the new government as well as the previous government of this country have allowed the United States to blackmail us economically and environmentally, and the Prime Minister has done absolutely nothing

to deal with the deadline the United States Congress and President Carter are now setting, which is December 6.
The Prime Minister has done nothing to cut through all our regulatory processes, nor has he done anything else to expedite the construction of a line, from which we will get absolutely no oil by American law, and I think we have to consider the fact that the Alyeska line is constructed. Tankers are moving down our coast at this point, and we have no legislation in place to protect Canadians. The government seems to be sitting idly by hoping, for some strange reason, that either Trans Mountain will suddenly develop itself or that Foothills will suddenly come into flower, knowing full well, as the Prime Minister did when he responded to me, that the National Energy Board had ruled Foothills deficient. Quite frankly, for a Prime Minister to stand up when the national regulatory agency has ruled a corporation deficient makes a mockery of the National Energy Board, and I make no bones about it. I think that is quite improper.
There are two further quotations I would like to give. One is from the U.S. Department of the Interior. It is a news release dated October 15, 1979. The quotation is found at the bottom of the page:
The permitting process is exclusively within our federal and state jurisdictions, thereby minimizing risk of potential delay resulting from obtaining approval from the Canadian government.
Quite clearly, the U.S. government is not interested in what this government has to say, and I must say neither the corporate sector nor the Liberal nor Conservative governments have actively pursued options of either tanker safety or minimizing of spills, and also in terms of spill clean-ups on the Pacific coast have not actively pursued the possibility of either moving oil from Alaska in the northern region by rail or having Petro-Canada initiate an involvement in the hearing process in order to pursue options other than simply allowing Foothills to have access to the corridor which is Canadian territory. It is in fact our jurisdiction, and we have regulatory processes in this country which should be heard and not be circumvented either by the Prime Minister or by anyone in the House.

subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-QUEBEC REFERENDUM-INQUIRY WHETHER PUBLIC SERVANTS WILL HAVE FREE VOTE
NATIONAL UNITY-QUEBEC REFERENDUM-INQUIRY WHETHER PUBLIC SERVANTS WILL HAVE FREE VOTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked for a debate this evening to discuss further the important question of the participation of federal public servants in the referendum campaign which will be held in Quebec next spring. On October 17 last I asked the Prime Minister whether his government would clarify the legal position of federal public servants in the referendum campaign. Mr. Speaker, freedom of speech is one of the fundamental rights of a free society. Each citizen, whether he is a public servant or not, must have this right and be able to exercise it. In the specific case of federal public servants, the oath of allegiance must not be viewed as forbidding this freedom of speech, especially in the case of a referendum and in view of the importance of this referendum for Canada as a whole.
There are, of course, certain restrictions to the freedom of speech of certain public servants involved through their duties in the development and implementation of government policies. However, to suggest that all public servants must be excluded from some sort of political involvement is not quite realistic. Most public servants are not involved in the development of policies and do not have access to the type of
Adjournment Debate
information which could threaten the government. Because of this, I believe that they should be excluded from section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act. These public servants should be free to take part in an election or a referendum campaign.
Indeed, this is essentially one of the recommendations of the committee on management and personnel, the famous D'Avig-non committee, which has been referred, so we are told, to a cabinet committee for consideration or indefinite shelving, despite the fact that the D'Avignon committee realistically and democratically recommended that most public servants be excluded from section 32 of the act and be free to take part in an election or a referendum.
It must be emphasized, however, that some officials must still be restricted from participating in elections in which I include the referendum, by reason of their responsibilities. It is to be regretted that the Progressive Conservative government could not recognize the soundness of the proposals put forward by the D'Avignon committee and accept the suggestion that there are three classes of civil servants: those who should be free to participate, those who should ask permission before they can do so, and those who should be restricted or completely forbidden from participating. I would have hoped that this government would not have hidden behind the screen of the Public Service Commission, that it would have shouldered its responsibilities and taken a position. Unfortunately it preferred to hide behind the Public Service Commission. Well, they hide behind this committee, that committee-everything is referred to committees. This is a no action government.
I know well that the Public Service Commission delivered an opinion yesterday based on legal advice given to them by justice. It was a recent one because I understand that they also had one, an official one-

-officieuse as we say in French, an informal opinion that was given to us in July or June last. According to my information, there is contradiction between the two and I wonder if in the spirit-

-of freedom of information, can the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) or his parliamentary secretary table those two legal opinions in the House so that members of Parliament and the Canadian public can see the difference between the opinion given unofficially in June or July saying no, they cannot participate, and the one given recently saying yes, they can participate? I want to know what the reasons were for this change of face or this change of mind.
Also I would like to take this opportunity to question the Prime Minister. A policy was announced last week regarding the contributions of Crown corporations which are supposed to be at arm's length and not under the auspices or under the

November 1, 1979
Adjournment Debate
control of the government. Instructions were given by the Prime Minister to Crown corporations, specifically Air Canada and Canadian National. He said, "You do not contribute funds to the support of the yes side of the referendum debate". I question these policies because they contradict somewhat the position of the Prime Minister regarding freedom of participation for the public service. On the one hand he said that they are free to go and participate in the referendum, and on the other hand he said to the Crown corporations which are supposed to be at arm's length with the government that no, they cannot participate. I would like to have from the parliamentary secretary a logical answer to this rather tenuous and rather difficult reasoning of the Prime Minister which, in my view, does not stand up to logic or reason.
Finally, I and many other Canadians are asking the Prime Minister: where is the leadership; where is the Canadian leadership; where is the Prime Minister on this question of the Quebec referendum? I speak to you, Mr. Speaker, as a Fran-co-Ontarian, not as a Quebecker, a fellow born and raised in Ontario. I am a fourth or fifth generation Ontarian. I believe strongly in this country of mine, Canada. [ would like to see my Prime Minister involved directly in this referendum campaign because I think the fabric of my country is at stake. I asked him, "Will you participate in this debate", and he said no.
I say to him, is he going to hide his head in the sand like an ostrich, is he going to shadow box with the Canadian public and then say, "You see, I won the referendum?" Is he going to suggest that because he shadow boxed himself into a situation where he did not know what was going to happen and in which he did not participate-is he then going to claim that he saved the country? Is this the kind of Prime Minister we are going to have, or is the parliamentary secretary going to tell me tonight that the Prime Minister will once and for all tell the people that he will vote no, and encourage all Canadians to say no to this referendum, or is he going to wishy-washy himself into a position which nobody understands yet? Will he please clarify the situation for me tonight?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have had some conversations in the past with the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), and tonight he again has done what he has done in the past and has done in the committee. He starts with one question and winds up with about six more. I am perfectly prepared to get him some other information if he wants that, but I think perhaps the fairest thing to do is deal with the original question which is before us for the late show, and which involves the matter that we promised we would deal with, providing the House, as we did at the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee, with the position given to us by the Public Service Commission after seeking legal opinion.

subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-QUEBEC REFERENDUM-INQUIRY WHETHER PUBLIC SERVANTS WILL HAVE FREE VOTE
speechtext: That is their opinion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-QUEBEC REFERENDUM-INQUIRY WHETHER PUBLIC SERVANTS WILL HAVE FREE VOTE
speechtext:
That is also the opinion of the government, and that is the position that needs to be made clear perhaps to the hon. member.
1 think the hon. member has a copy of this position, but for the record I should perhaps read some of it so that it is clear. It states in part:
-the commission has come to the conclusion that as the law now stands it is possible for federal public servants to engage in some referendum activities without violating section 32.
Without reading all of the letter perhaps I should read the caveat clauses, which are these:
-federal employees must recognize that there may well be partisan party work going on during the campaign.
As the hon. member knows, it is that section in relation to partisan party work to which we are referring.
It states:
-there may well be partisan party work going on during the campaign. Therefore, the commission considers it appropriate to advise federal employees to take special care and use their own discretion to ensure that any activities they undertake do not actually engage them, as such, in partisan party activity.
Furthermore, the commission must also emphasize that in general, federal employees, in deciding whether to become involved and, if so, in deciding what the specific nature of that involvement might be, should at all times be conscious of their obligation not to engage in activity which might adversely affect their ability to perform their functions in the federal public service in an effective and credible manner.
We also emphasize that. It then continues:
The foregoing consideration should be of particular importance to senior federal employees, especially those directly involved in. . . policy advice to the government.
Finally, in all instances, employees are advised to consult with their deputy heads-
I think that is perfectly clear and I know of no other position taken by the Public Service Commission, to which the hon. member alludes. If he can give me some evidence that there is,
I would be happy to search it out, but I do not know of any.
Our position on why Crown corporations should not make financial contributions to either side of the referendum campaign is probably most easily understood as being the same reason that we feel strongly about the rights and privileges ol senior public servants, to which the hon. member refers. We suggest that the act that governs the behaviour of individuals does not prohibit activity in the referendum, subject to some limits. I suggest that it is equally appropriate to say that federal Crown corporations, which belong in some sense to all Canadians, are in a difficult position if they take a position one way or the other.
There is a question as to what the federal government's role should be in this-
